# Local demo inventory

This note separates unauthenticated process-memory behavior from Firebase-backed owner-sandbox behavior. It is not an acceptance rubric or a production-readiness claim.

## Local process-memory mode

- Selected when the API runs without a Firebase project ID. The browser shows `LOCAL PREVIEW`; there is no user sign-in boundary. Directory/workflow/raw records are shared by callers of that local API process and reset when the process stops.
- Synthetic employee create/update is limited to the allowed display fields. IDs are server-generated. New employees receive no schedule mapping.
- Raw attendance queries are read-only as a view; the explicitly authorized **create-only** demo form is the exception. It accepts an existing mapped synthetic employee, date, time-in, and time-out. The server supplies the existing schedule ID and `DEMO` label; the store enforces unique schedule/date and `timeIn <= timeOut`. No correction, delete, schedule assignment, attendance classification, hours, or pay is added.
- Leave/ticket workflows are synthetic, process-memory records with their existing submit/cancel limits; no reviewer, approval, resolution, or delivery action is present.
- The temporary statutory calculator takes fictional browser inputs and is not persisted or connected to attendance, employees, or a payroll API.
- The read-only raw attendance calendar (including its two-date inclusive filter), employee linked-record detail and searchable/mapped-filterable/sortable stored count summary with visible/all CSV, cross-module search, workflow type filters, visible/all CSV exports, and JSON workspace export use the same local demo service. The JSON export includes only the current synthetic records and marks `hoursCalculated:false`, `payrollIncluded:false`; search/export issue reads only.

## Firebase user-sandbox mode

- The app requires Firebase Email/Password sign-in when client configuration is complete; API reads/writes use the caller's user-scoped paths and existing published rules.
- Employee display fields and owner-scoped workflow routes retain their previously accepted limits. The employee-linked record view, raw attendance calendar, cross-module search, and JSON bundle use user-scoped reads.
- **Firebase attendance stays read-only.** `POST /api/attendance` is rejected with `403` before a storage service is accessed. No Firebase attendance write has been introduced.
- No user roles, employee-account mapping, supervisor/team boundaries, approvals, schedule assignment, attendance calculations, payroll inputs, or persisted pay/payslip workflow are introduced by this slice.

## Local acceptance evidence

- Java domain/service checks cover mapping, fixed day type, unique schedule/date, time order, and unmapped employee rejection.
- Java API integration checks cover the local `201` response metadata, duplicate `409`, invalid `400`, fixed server mapping/classification, client-supplied schedule rejection, and Firebase-mode `403`.
- Browser E2E covers successful local capture, duplicate/mapping/time-order rejection, raw calendar display, employee-linked rows, type-filtered visible exports, cross-module search, JSON export contents, and read-only HTTP methods for bundle/search.
- Latest fully run checks and their counts are recorded in `README.md` and `docs/peer-parity-roadmap.md`.
# Source-grounded acceptance baseline (draft)

**Purpose:** record observable pass/fail behavior already implemented and define safe candidate acceptance criteria before tailoring. This is a working baseline, **not an approved rubric interpretation**. No standalone active MO-IT110 grading rubric was identified among the supplied files in the workspace; the older MO-IT108/107 documents and peer submissions inform scope, while the Terminal Assessment proposal is treated as placeholder material rather than an authoritative detailed specification.

**Scope rules:** fictional data only; use the signed-in user's sandbox in Firebase mode; keep ordinary local-preview persistence explicitly process-memory; do not treat inferred attendance/payroll rules, peer-project choices, employee-to-account identity, reviewer authority, or access boundaries as approved policy. At the user's direction, a clearly labelled 2026 monthly statutory preview is now available with synthetic inputs only; its rules are isolated in a changeable module and it has no API/Firestore/payslip path. Attendance-based or persistent payroll, approvals, and reviewer controls remain gated. See `docs/candidate-policy-review.md`. The user-published development rules remain unchanged.

# Candidate policy review from prior submissions and current references

**Status: research and changeable demo profile; not approved production policy.** The user invited disclosed candidate inference and specifically authorized a temporary 2026 statutory preview. This document records prior-work candidates and risks. A synthetic-input monthly preview is enabled in the app, but this document does not authorize attendance-hour derivation, saved payroll/payslips, approvals, or role-based access. No official MotorPH payroll rulebook or active grading rubric was found in the supplied set.

## 1. What the inspected MO-IT110 peer implementation says

The supplied peer review copy at `/home/user/repo_review/full_repo/testingester-main/6/-/` contains an explicit, testable candidate model:

- `src/motorph/model/AttendanceRecord.java`: first cutoff is days 1–15; second cutoff is day 16 through actual month end. Login from 08:00 through 08:10 is treated as 08:00; logout after 17:00 is capped at 17:00. It calculates elapsed time directly from those adjusted times and does **not** subtract a meal interval.
- `src/motorph/service/PayrollProcessor.java`: the first cutoff has no deductions and net equals cutoff gross. On the second cutoff, it computes monthly contributions from the combined two-cutoff gross, computes withholding tax after those contributions, and subtracts the whole monthly deduction amount from the second-cutoff gross (floored at zero). Allowances are shown on the second-cutoff slip but excluded from net in that implementation.
- `src/motorph/model/Employee.java`: gross is hourly rate times the calculated minutes. The course-project fixtures also supply semi-monthly and hourly rates.
- The peer has substantial tests and CP2 compatibility comparisons, but its own behavior is still an implementation choice, not an authoritative MotorPH payroll rule.

**Important defect/risk found in that candidate:** an 08:00–17:00 record yields nine elapsed hours because the code caps at 17:00 but deducts no lunch. DOLE's source says normal work hours do not exceed eight hours a day and requires at least a 60-minute meal period off work; a pair of in/out times without a meal record cannot distinguish the unpaid break. The peer rule must not be copied as an hours-worked or overtime algorithm without resolving that mismatch.

The supplied peer review also records 473 of 476 comparison rows and 14 of 14 cutoff summaries matching the CP2 output; three row differences were ₱0.01 due to floating/half-centavo behavior. That is compatibility evidence, not legal-compliance evidence. See `/home/user/repo_review/submission-comprehensive-report.md` and `/home/user/repo_review/submission-feature-pseudocode.md` for the review context. No peer employee or government-ID data was copied into this app or document.

A public MO-IT110 repository surfaced the same 1–15 / 16–month-end pattern and second-cutoff deduction convention, but explicitly says its payroll tables/thresholds are copied from CP2 rather than independently verified. Treat it as corroboration of a *course-project convention*, not a company policy: https://github.com/fdtan/MO-IT110_OOP-MS2_TanFD.

## 2. Current official statutory references located

These sources can support statutory-component research, but they do not establish MotorPH's attendance import, pay-period, allowance, leave, or role policy:

| Component | Source finding | Boundary before implementation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| SSS | The SSS site publishes its contribution schedule effective Jan. 1, 2025: 15% total on MSC up to ₱35,000, split 5% employee / 10% employer; EC is employer-only. The schedule also distinguishes the MPF portion above ₱20,000. | Use the circular/table and verify every bracket and rounding boundary. Do not assume a new 2026 table without a newer official circular. |
| PhilHealth | The 2026 advisory states the 5% contribution rate effective Jan. 2025, with ₱10,000 floor and ₱100,000 ceiling. The 2025 employer advisory says use monthly basic salary and excludes overtime, allowances, 13th-month pay, bonuses and specified absence/undertime reductions from that base. | Confirm the formal-sector share split and exact payroll-period deduction method against the applicable circular. |
| Pag-IBIG | Circular 460 raises the Maximum Fund Salary to ₱10,000 effective February 2024; the employee rate is 1% at fund salary ≤₱1,500 and 2% above, while the employer rate is 2%. | Confirm applicable employee category and effective date; don't extrapolate to voluntary/other member types. |
| BIR withholding | Annex E to RR 11-2018 publishes daily, weekly, semi-monthly and monthly tables effective Jan. 1, 2023 onward. | The chosen tax base, payroll-period method, taxable allowances/benefits, year-end adjustment and rounding need explicit tests. A monthly-only example is not a semi-monthly payroll specification. |
| Hours/premiums | DOLE's official materials specify an eight-hour normal workday, a minimum 60-minute meal period off work, and statutory overtime/night/rest-day/holiday provisions. | The attendance schema lacks meal punches, a defined `dayType` enum, and an authoritative schedule/holiday assignment. Those facts must be supplied or explicitly selected as demo assumptions. |

## 3. A net-pay reference found online — useful, but not a drop-in payroll engine

`ph-payroll` is the strongest technical reference located for statutory components: its README says it uses exact decimal arithmetic, effective-dated rules, source circulars, and fails closed outside covered periods; it documents support from **2026-01** because the 2026 PhilHealth rule is the most recent component. Its scope is monthly basic pay plus statutory contributions/tax, not attendance-hour computation, MotorPH's cutoff handling, leave treatment, or a payslip workflow. It is MIT-licensed and asks users to verify results before relying on it: https://github.com/earnieacts/ph-payroll.

### Documented synthetic example from that reference

For monthly basic pay of ₱25,000, the library documents employee deductions of SSS ₱1,250, PhilHealth ₱625, Pag-IBIG ₱200, withholding tax ₱313.75, and net ₱22,611.25. A manual annualized arithmetic check gives taxable monthly income ₱22,925; annualized ₱275,100; 15% of the ₱25,100 annual amount above ₱250,000 is ₱3,765, or ₱313.75 per month. This is a reference example only—not this app's result or an approved MotorPH payslip.

Two caveats need reconciliation before adoption:

1. The BIR Annex E monthly table uses rounded peso breakpoints (₱20,833 and 15% above that), which yields ₱313.80 for ₱22,925 when read directly. The library's annualized method gives ₱313.75. The ₱0.05 difference needs a verified BIR-period/rounding interpretation and an independent approved example.
2. In the library source, `employerCost` is the sum of employer contributions (₱3,355 in its ₱25,000 example), not basic salary plus those contributions. Do not display that field as total employer payroll cost without changing/renaming it.

A second 2026 calculator repository also advertises complete deductions and net pay, but the repository surfaced with a single commit and no comparable validation evidence. It is a secondary cross-check, not a preferred authority: https://github.com/tenzerodev/rdcruz-ph-payroll.

## 6. Re-review of the user's database design and later calculator work

The user's ctxt.io document is the **MO-IT107 database design/data dictionary**, not a database file or a set of calculation rules. It does, however, lay out a useful storage model that the earlier review had not connected to a working calculation pipeline:

- `Rates` and `Tax Table` are intended as changeable reference tables; the design mentions a rate `implementationYear`, although this field is missing from the linked Data Dictionary and the design's own key constraints disagree.
- `Government Deductibles` separates monthly employer contribution, employee contribution, and withholding tax.
- `Contributions` stores SSS, PhilHealth, and Pag-IBIG amounts separately for `Employee` and `Employer`.
- `Payroll`, `Payslip`, `Earnings`, `Deductibles`, `Other Transactions`, `Government Tally`, and `Summary` cover the intended input/output and reporting areas. Payslip includes a start/end period and gross income.
- The related DFD describes the order of operations: timesheet validation → wage/adjustments → government deductibles → basic payroll computation → payslip → monthly summary. The System Admin has a rate-update flow.

That design is valuable for the **mechanics before calculation**, but it contains no actual rates, effective date ranges, formula, rounding policy, or worked expected values. In particular, the tax table is not explicit about whether each row is monthly, semi-monthly, or another withholding period, and the monthly government-deduction key shown in the design has no year component. The user-provided full synthesis likewise warns that the PDFs do not state statutory values or arithmetic. The design should be versioned and reconciled before it is used as a persistent production schema.

A different older SQLite file exists in peer folder 1 (`/home/user/repo_review/full_repo/testingester-main/1/-/myMotorPhdb.db`). I inspected its table definitions only—not any records—and found `Users`, `Allowance`, `Salary_Deduction`, `EmployeeAudit`, and `Employee_info`, not the normalized Rates/Tax Table/Government Deductibles design in the ctxt link. It is not a source of verified statutory rates.

### A later prior project did tackle the calculation pipeline

The supplied folder-9 review copy, `/home/user/repo_review/full_repo/testingester-main/9/-/oop/`, contains an actual `PayrollCalculator` orchestrator and separate SSS, PhilHealth, Pag-IBIG, and withholding-tax calculators. Its pipeline is:

1. derive gross as worked days × hourly rate × 8;
2. calculate employee/employer statutory items;
3. calculate withholding after employee statutory contributions;
4. calculate net and build an immutable payroll record.

Its NOTES and console tests report this pipeline exercised. But the formulas are hard-coded as Java `double` constants and the source XLSX matrices cited by its verification note were on a personal Windows path, not among the supplied files. The source values are **not a current 2026 ruleset**:

- SSS caps the employee share at ₱1,125, which predates the 2025 schedule (2026 uses the current schedule effective January 2025: 5% employee / 10% employer on MSC up to ₱35,000, plus employer-only EC).
- PhilHealth uses 3%, a ₱10,000 floor/₱60,000 ceiling and a 50/50 split; the current direct-contributor advisory for formal-sector MBS gives 5%, ₱10,000 floor/₱100,000 ceiling, with allowances and overtime excluded from the MBS base.
- Pag-IBIG caps at ₱100, reflecting the former ₱5,000 MFS; Circular 460 moved the MFS ceiling to ₱10,000 effective February 2024, allowing up to ₱200 per side.
- Its first taxable monthly BIR band uses 20%; Annex E uses 15% from ₱20,833 to ₱33,332. The prior project also does not make a semi-monthly tax table part of its calculator API.

A separate folder-7 `ContributionCalculator.java` also computes semi-monthly values, but doubles the pay-period input to a monthly proxy and reuses old CP2 schedules: SSS max ₱1,125, PhilHealth 1.5% employee amount with ₱900 cap, Pag-IBIG cap ₱100, and a 20% first taxable band. Its payroll code labels overtime pricing as temporary pending confirmation. Folder 3 is even simpler (flat 4.5% SSS, 2% PhilHealth, ₱100 Pag-IBIG, no tax schedule). These show earlier mechanical exploration, but none supply a current validated 2026 profile.

The older folder-6 implementation is even more explicitly a CP2/course-project compatibility profile, not a 2026 statutory table. Neither implementation was copied into the current app.

## 7. Temporary 2026 module now in this prototype

Following the user's instruction, a **client-side-only, synthetic-input preview** has been added to the Payroll workspace. It is deliberately isolated and replaceable:

- Change rates, thresholds, table bands, sources, or the profile ID in `web/payroll-rules-2026.js`.
- Calculation logic is pure and separated in `web/payroll-preview-2026.js`; amounts are parsed and calculated in integer centavos (`BigInt`), not binary floating point.
- `web/payroll-preview-ui.js` only renders the submitted values and result. It sends no payroll API request, reads no employee or attendance record, and persists nothing in Firebase or local storage.
- Current scope is **monthly 2026 statutory preview only**. It requires separate cash-pay, SSS compensation, PhilHealth MBS, Pag-IBIG Fund Salary, and taxable-compensation inputs. That prevents the preview from silently assuming all legal contribution/tax bases are identical.
- It separates employee deductions from employer costs, includes the current SSS employer-only EC amount, uses the BIR **monthly** Annex E table with a provisional half-up centavo rounding rule, and blocks a negative net rather than emitting a negative payslip.
- It does not create/pay a payroll, resolve salary conversion, attendance hours, overtime, leave/holiday earnings, deductions between cutoffs, tax annualisation/adjustment, benefit exemptions, employees, or payslips.

For a fully synthetic ₱25,000 monthly example using ₱25,000 for each input base, this profile produces: SSS employee ₱1,250; SSS employer SS/MPF ₱2,500 plus EC ₱30; PhilHealth ₱625 each; Pag-IBIG ₱200 each; taxable base after employee shares ₱22,925; monthly BIR withholding ₱313.80; net estimate ₱22,611.20; employer statutory contributions ₱3,355; gross plus those employer contributions ₱28,355.00. The difference from `ph-payroll`'s documented ₱22,611.25 is the disclosed monthly-table versus annualized-tax method/rounding difference; the sandbox uses the published BIR monthly table for its monthly mode, not the library result.

The input boundaries and the editable monthly calculation are now covered in `test/web/payroll-preview-2026.test.js`; a browser E2E check confirms the result and that no payroll API call is made. The profile remains a **temporary estimate**, not an approved payroll policy or statutory compliance guarantee.

- SSS's official contribution page links Circular 2024-006 / the schedule effective Jan. 2025: 15% total on MSC (5% employee / 10% employer), up to ₱35,000 MSC; EC is employer-only and set at ₱10 or ₱30 by MSC band: https://www.sss.gov.ph/pay-contribution/
- PhilHealth Advisory PA2025-0002: 5% effective Jan. 2025; monthly basic salary floor ₱10,000 / ceiling ₱100,000; allowances, overtime, 13th-month pay, bonuses and similar items excluded from employer MBS: https://www.philhealth.gov.ph/advisories/2025/PA2025-0002.pdf
- Pag-IBIG Circular 460: employee 1% at Fund Salary up to ₱1,500, 2% above; employer 2%; MFS ₱10,000, effective Feb. 2024: https://www.pagibigfund.gov.ph/documents/Circular%20No.%20460%20-%20Guidelines%20on%20the%20Pag-IBIG%20Fund's%20Implementation%20of%20Increase%20in%20the%20MFS%20Effective%20February%202024.pdf

# Legacy MotorPH coursework → current MS2 traceability

**Purpose:** use the user's earlier MO-IT108 MotorPH documents to clarify the current prototype without silently expanding its approved scope. These are earlier-course sources (A.Y. 2024–2025), not the active MO-IT110 MS2 rubric. They can inform design and requirements mapping, but do not override the current boundary: only an isolated synthetic 2026 monthly statutory preview is enabled; attendance-based or persisted payroll remains disabled.

## Sources inspected

- `/home/user/uploads/MO-IT108 - 1st Milestone_ Requirements Analysis Document of MotorPH Payroll System H1103 Torres, A. (1).pdf` — a requirements document with ten functional-requirement groups and non-functional requirements.
- `/home/user/uploads/MO-IT108 - 2nd Milestone_ System Design Document of MotorPH Payroll System H1103 Torres, A. (1).pdf` — module descriptions, scenarios, data concepts, and an RBAC matrix.
- `/home/user/uploads/MO-IT108 - Terminal Assessment_ Business Technology Proposal for MotorPH Payroll System H1103 Torres, A..pdf` — a broad technology proposal. Several major sections still contain template prompts/placeholders, so treat it as vision/context rather than an approved detailed specification.

## What the legacy documents clarify

### Attendance view

The MO-IT108 Requirements Analysis says employees can view attendance metrics over a date range, defaulting from the earliest to latest available record. The System Design expands this into daily logs and counts for present, absent, tardy, overtime, undertime, and leave usage. It also names concepts such as `ClockInStatus`, `ShiftStartTime`, `ShiftEndTime`, `GracePeriod`, `AttendanceTag`, `TotalWorked`, `WorkHourTag`, `AbsentCount`, `PresentCount`, `TardyCount`, `OvertimeHours`, `UndertimeHours`, `LeaveTaken`, and `LeaveBalance`.

This clarifies the intended *shape* of the attendance screen, but not a complete calculation policy. The documents do not provide actual grace-period values, the absence threshold, break treatment, rounding, overnight-shift handling, missing-punch corrections, timezone policy, overtime triggers, or a worked expected example. One field is described as `TotalWorked` based on clock-in/out, but that alone does not settle those rules. Therefore the app now defaults the raw-record filter to the selected synthetic employee's earliest and latest available dates; the user may narrow the inclusive range. This is a data-range convenience, **not** a payroll period, and no hour/category totals are derived.

### Payroll snapshot and pay cycle

The legacy System Design lists proposed snapshot fields such as `PayrollCycleStart`, `PayrollCycleEnd`, `HourlyWage`, `RegHours`, `OTHours`, `PTOHours`, holiday hours/shifts, incentives, tax, other deductions, gross/net pay, and a snapshot timestamp. The Requirements Analysis also names wage components, incentives, statutory/other deductions, payroll reports, and payslip distribution.

These are useful field names and workflow hints, not complete formulas or full current policy. The documents do not give exact semi-monthly cut-off dates, salary-to-hourly conversion, attendance rules, benefits treatment, rounding policy, or a complete expected payslip. A separate synthetic 2026 statutory preview now covers only monthly SSS/PhilHealth/Pag-IBIG and BIR withholding; employee-linked salary snapshots, attendance calculations, saved payroll, and payslips remain disabled.

### Identity and roles

The legacy documents describe Employee, Supervisor/Lead, HR, Payroll Staff, and System Admin roles. Their RBAC matrix distinguishes self/team access, HR/Payroll actions, and approvals for government details; the requirements also call for 2FA and branch-aware access. The current prototype has Firebase Email/Password sign-in and an isolated per-user synthetic sandbox only. It does **not** implement 2FA, branch routing, team membership, HR/Payroll roles, production PII handling, or the legacy RBAC matrix. No real employee information is permitted.

| 5. Tickets | **Partial, owner-scoped create/cancel** | Fictional ticket submission/cancel and queue labels for overtime, leave, timesheet, payroll, HR, and technical support; nothing is delivered or resolved. Published user-scoped Firestore rules were live-smoke-tested for ticket create/cancel. |
| 6. Leave tracker/calendar | **Partial, owner-scoped create/cancel** | Validated fictional request submit/cancel plus a display-only calendar of submitted/cancelled date ranges; no balance/accrual, approval, payroll treatment, or approved leave calendar. Published user-scoped Firestore rules were live-smoke-tested for leave create/cancel. |
| 7. Team management | **Partial read-only roster** | Shows synthetic directory records; no team membership, schedules, supervisor scope, or approval workflow. |
| 8. HR handling | **Partial synthetic directory maintenance** | Signed-in Firebase users can create/update allowlisted fictional directory fields in their own sandbox; local mode is unauthenticated process memory. No HR role, schedule assignment, delete, onboarding/offboarding, or sensitive PII. |
| 9. Payroll supervision | **Preview-only partial** | A separate synthetic monthly statutory calculator exists; no employee-linked payroll, adjustments, approvals, payslips, or reports. |
| 10. Payroll distribution | **Not implemented** | No payslip generation, email delivery, retry handling, or distribution status. |

## Percent estimate: two different denominators

There is no single valid percentage “against the submitted folders”: those projects have different feature sets, tech stacks, and course scopes, and several are near-duplicates. The ranges below are **feature-completeness estimates, not a grade or quality score**.

- **Agreed current Tasks 1–3 scope: about 85–90%.** Task 1's live Firebase proof is complete. Task 2's browser sign-in and employee selection are verified on localhost, with the exact Arena preview-origin authorization still unverified. Task 3's employee/date inputs and raw-record path are complete; derived attendance-hour totals remain gated because their algorithm and test oracle are missing. The separate monthly statutory preview does not enable attendance-based payroll.
- **Full legacy MO-IT108 functional breadth: roughly 25–35% represented, but less operationally complete.** The app has a real sign-in/data foundation, limited owner-scoped synthetic directory editing, local-only create-only raw attendance for mapped synthetic employees (Firebase remains read-only), and owner-scoped leave/ticket create/cancel routes (published user-scoped Firestore rules live-smoke-tested for leave/ticket create/cancel). These limited workflows do not include reviewers or approvals. Clocking, leave balances/approvals/approved calendars, delivered and resolved tickets, actual team/supervisor management, HR lifecycle operations, full payroll calculations (beyond the temporary statutory preview), payslips, reports, RBAC/2FA, and production operations remain unimplemented.
- **Compared with the more complete numbered submissions (especially folders 6 and 9): roughly 25–35% of end-to-end feature breadth.** This prototype is stronger in live Firebase Auth/Firestore integration, browser accessibility/responsiveness, and current test evidence; those reference projects include end-to-end payroll engines/results and broader workflows that this app deliberately does not yet have; the temporary monthly statutory calculator is not an attendance-to-payslip engine. Compared with the smallest procedural/demo submissions, the comparison can reverse because this project already has a live web/data foundation.

The largest gap to “parity” is not another Firebase feature: it is the **unbuilt payroll/business workflow** (validated attendance summaries, approved pay rules, payroll results/payslips, and applicable roles). Do not close that gap by importing unverified formulas from another submission.

*Two front ends use the data differently:**

- `Console.TACP2` is a terminal workflow: login with employee number/last name; view profile, daily attendance, weekly hours and payroll. It downloads published Google Sheets CSV over HTTP, so it depends on internet access and the sheet schema.
- The Swing UI starts from `GUI.LogIn` and proceeds to `GUI.MainMenu`. It uses the bundled local CSVs and has profile, attendance, payroll, employee table and employee add/update/delete screens.

The `Backend/` package contains employee/attendance records, CSV loading, payroll processors (regular, final-pay and 13th-month variants), statutory deduction calculators, regular/holiday overtime classes, plus leave and payslip-dispute domain classes. The regular payroll processor uses attendance totals and a `Payslip`; deduction types are separate classes. The GUI exposes employee dispute submission and a payroll-side review/resolve/reject frame.

**Caveats:** leave records shown by the GUI are explicitly hard-coded sample rows because there is no leave data file. Payslip disputes live in a singleton in-memory list, not persistent storage, so the records disappear on process exit. The payroll-side dispute frame itself notes role authorization is not implemented. The console path fetches external sheets; the GUI path reads local data—do not confuse them as one identical data flow. This is a CP2-labeled comparison project, not an MS1-approved design by evidence in this folder.

## Folder 9 — documented MO-IT110 Team 3 CP2-to-OOP project

**Location:** `9/-/`. This is the most documented folder: README, old `README.CP2.md`, `SETUP.md`, `oop/NOTES.md`, parity/matrix reports, console/test outputs, a QA workbook, and code. It has 15 Java files in the original GUI `src/`, 13 in `oop/src/` (12 backend classes plus `ConsoleBackendTest`), and 3 test/probe files. The README identifies the OOP work as MO-IT110 OOP Team 3, and identifies the CP2 baseline as MO-IT103 Group 4. Those are source-repository statements, not confirmation of the current user's authorship or reuse permission.

**Two connected source roots:**

- `src/motorphemployee/` is the earlier CP2 Swing app (login, landing screen, dashboard, employee forms, leave screens and related UI). Its data remains in CSV.
- `oop/src/motorphemployee/oop/` is the OOP payroll backend. `Person` → `Employee` → `RegularEmployee`/`ProbationaryEmployee` is the data hierarchy; `GovernmentContributionCalculator` has concrete contribution/tax calculators; `AttendanceLog` models attendance; `PayrollCalculator` coordinates employee + attendance + calculators and produces `PayrollRecord`.
- `ConsoleBackendTest` provides a console test harness before GUI integration. The GUI's `MainMenu`/`Dashboard` were rewired to call the OOP backend rather than compute payroll themselves.
- `AttendanceRepository` loads the real timecard CSV and supplies worked-day data to the payroll flow. `LeaveService` processes approval/rejection and writes the related CSV files; `LeaveForm` still has a separate direct append path noted as an open issue.

**How the feature sequence works:** employee/attendance CSV → `AttendanceRepository`/`AttendanceLog` → `PayrollCalculator` → contribution calculators → immutable `PayrollRecord` → GUI display. The README and notes describe preserving the CP2 UI while replacing duplicated calculations with one backend. They also document changes to modal popups, attendance sourcing and the add-employee form; these are later implementation refinements beyond the core OOP concept demonstration.

**The explicit module link:** the README maps W2 to encapsulation, W3 to abstraction, W4 to inheritance and W5 to polymorphism, and describes MS1 as 16 unique classes, 35 CRC rows and 97 method rows. It says MS2 implements 12 of the 16 design classes; `Credentials`, `LeaveRequest`, `LeaveManagement` and `HRManager` remain design-only. It states the GUI should present only, payroll math should live in the backend, and backend console tests should precede GUI integration. The repo includes official-matrix verification and CP2-parity evidence; the README says some deduction results intentionally differ from CP2 because the OOP version follows the official matrices, while gross pay matches the CP2 baseline. Do not transfer those tax/contribution assumptions to your assignment without checking its current approved rules.

The README reports 91/91 backend checks and several other dated test/GUI evidence logs. I have not rerun them. The QA workbook in this folder is named for a CP2 Group 4 QA submission; it should not be mistaken for proof that the OOP source was authored by the current user.

**Course connection:** the strongest visible MS1→MS2 teaching example in the repository because its own README and code comments map the OOP concepts and design artifacts into implementation. It is useful for studying the mapping, not automatically reusable submission material.

## How these projects relate to the course modules

There are two levels of evidence, and they should not be conflated:

1. **Explicit labels in the files:** folder 3 says COMPROG1/Terminal Assessment; folders 4, 5 and 8 are CP2-labeled or path-identified; folders 6 and 9 explicitly describe MO-IT110 MS2/OOP work; folder 2 is labelled MO-IT110 OOP but lacks an included MS1 package tying its classes to an approved design.
2. **Conceptual fit:** CSV and database folders illustrate data/file I/O; Swing folders illustrate GUI event handling; model/service/backend folders illustrate OOP decomposition; folders 6 and 9 demonstrate inheritance/abstraction/polymorphism; tests and comparison reports illustrate verification.

From the MO-IT110 Modules 02–09 handout previously reviewed, the project focus is the MotorPH payroll application and its employee/attendance data; the handout does **not** prescribe one particular MotorPH spreadsheet tab as the project base. The numbered folders themselves generally do not record a reliable one-to-one mapping from a particular feature to a specific module number. For that reason this report maps folders to the explicit milestones/concepts above rather than inventing claims like “folder 4 is Module 6.” The clearest official milestone relationship is folder 9's stated MS1 design → MS2 implementation, with folder 6 as a separate MS2 example.

## Cross-folder conclusions and safe study order

- **Folders 2 and 5 are the same practical implementation** despite their different README labels; study one, not both, unless comparing the packaging/attribution differences.
- **Folders 4, 5 and 8 are alternative CP2-style systems**, not evidence of the user's personal CP2 app. Their persistence choices differ (CSV vs MySQL vs CSV/online sheet), and their features are not interchangeable.
- **Folder 9 is the best source here for tracing explicit MS1 concepts into MS2 code**, while folder 6 is a smaller, separate implementation example of the same design-to-implementation idea. Both need authorship/permission confirmation before graded use.
- **Folder 3 is a separate CP1-style reference**, not proof that the user has a CP2 app.
- **Folders 1 and 7 have unclear provenance/course stage.** Use them only as generic technical comparisons until a mentor or repository author confirms their context.

Suggested reading order for understanding—not copying—is: **3** (small console building blocks) → **one CP2 project** (4, 5 or 8; folder 4 is the clearest package-separated example) → **6** (smaller MS2 separation) → **9** (most explicit MS1-to-MS2 mapping and evidence). For your own MS1, start from the official rubric and your actual approved project requirements; use another folder only as a comparison after confirming permission and fit.

name: documentation-and-adrs

Use when you need to document an architecture decision (ADR) or the reasoning behind a design choice, when changing public APIs, shipping features, or when you need to record context that future engineers and agents will need to understand the codebase.

# Documentation and ADRs

## Overview

Document decisions, not just code. The most valuable documentation captures the *why* — the context, constraints, and trade-offs that led to a decision. Code shows *what* was built; documentation explains *why it was built this way* and *what alternatives were considered*. This context is essential for future humans and agents working in the codebase.

## When to Use

- Making a significant architectural decision
- Choosing between competing approaches
- Adding or changing a public API
- Shipping a feature that changes user-facing behavior
- Onboarding new team members (or agents) to the project
- When you find yourself explaining the same thing repeatedly

**When NOT to use:** Don't document obvious code. Don't add comments that restate what the code already says. Don't write docs for throwaway prototypes.

## Architecture Decision Records (ADRs)

ADRs capture the reasoning behind significant technical decisions. They're the highest-value documentation you can write.

### When to Write an ADR

- Choosing a framework, library, or major dependency
- Designing a data model or database schema
- Selecting an authentication strategy
- Deciding on an API architecture (REST vs. GraphQL vs. tRPC)
- Choosing between build tools, hosting platforms, or infrastructure
- Any decision that would be expensive to reverse

### Match the existing convention first

Before creating an ADR, inspect the available repository context for an established convention — existing ADRs, project instructions, and ADR-related configuration or tooling (e.g. an `.adr-dir` file). An established convention overrides the defaults below. Match:

- **Location and format** — e.g. `docs/adr/*.md`, `Documentation/Decisions/*.rst`, a MADR layout, or an `adr-tools` setup. Match the existing directory, file extension, and markup (Markdown vs reStructuredText).
- **Numbering and naming** — continue the existing sequence and filename pattern (`ADR-004-Title.rst`, `0004-title.md`, …); don't restart at 001 or introduce a second scheme.
- **Section headings** — reuse the project's heading set rather than imposing this template's.

If the available evidence conflicts, surface the conflict rather than silently introducing another scheme. Only when no convention can be established do you apply the default below.

### ADR Template

Store ADRs in `docs/decisions/` with sequential numbering (unless the project already uses another location — see above):

```markdown
# ADR-001: Use PostgreSQL for primary database

## Status
Proposed | Accepted | Superseded by ADR-XXX | Deprecated

## Date
2025-01-15

## Context
We need a primary database for the task management application. Key requirements:
- Relational data model (users, tasks, teams with relationships)
- ACID transactions for task state changes
- Support for full-text search on task content
- Managed hosting available (for small team, limited ops capacity)

## Decision
Use PostgreSQL with Prisma ORM.

## Alternatives Considered

### MongoDB
- Pros: Flexible schema, easy to start with
- Cons: Our data is inherently relational; would need to manage relationships manually
- Rejected: Relational data in a document store leads to complex joins or data duplication

### SQLite
- Pros: Zero configuration, embedded, fast for reads
- Cons: Limited concurrent write support, no managed hosting for production
- Rejected: Not suitable for multi-user web application in production

### MySQL
- Pros: Mature, widely supported
- Cons: PostgreSQL has better JSON support, full-text search, and ecosystem tooling
- Rejected: PostgreSQL is the better fit for our feature requirements

## Consequences
- Prisma provides type-safe database access and migration management
- We can use PostgreSQL's full-text search instead of adding Elasticsearch
- Team needs PostgreSQL knowledge (standard skill, low risk)
- Hosting on managed service (Supabase, Neon, or RDS)
```

### ADR Lifecycle

```
PROPOSED → ACCEPTED → (SUPERSEDED or DEPRECATED)
```

- **Don't delete old ADRs.** They capture historical context.
- When a decision changes, write a new ADR that references and supersedes the old one.

## Inline Documentation

### When to Comment

Comment the *why*, not the *what*:

```typescript
// BAD: Restates the code
// Increment counter by 1
counter += 1;

// GOOD: Explains non-obvious intent
// Rate limit uses a fixed window that opens on the first request after the
// previous one expires, not on a clock schedule. Known gap: a client can spend
// the full limit just before a reset and again just after (2x in a moment)
if (now - windowStart > WINDOW_SIZE_MS) {
  counter = 0;
  windowStart = now;
}
```

### When NOT to Comment

```typescript
// Don't comment self-explanatory code
function calculateTotal(items: CartItem[]): number {
  return items.reduce((sum, item) => sum + item.price * item.quantity, 0);
}

// Don't leave TODO comments for things you should just do now
// TODO: add error handling  ← Just add it

// Don't leave commented-out code
// const oldImplementation = () => { ... }  ← Delete it, git has history
```

### Document Known Gotchas

```typescript
/**
 * IMPORTANT: This function must be called before the first render.
 * If called after hydration, it causes a flash of unstyled content
 * because the theme context isn't available during SSR.
 *
 * See ADR-003 for the full design rationale.
 */
export function initializeTheme(theme: Theme): void {
  // ...
}
```

## API Documentation

For public APIs (REST, GraphQL, library interfaces):

### Inline with Types (Preferred for TypeScript)

```typescript
/**
 * Creates a new task.
 *
 * @param input - Task creation data (title required, description optional)
 * @returns The created task with server-generated ID and timestamps
 * @throws {ValidationError} If title is empty or exceeds 200 characters
 * @throws {AuthenticationError} If the user is not authenticated
 *
 * @example
 * const task = await createTask({ title: 'Buy groceries' });
 * console.log(task.id); // "task_abc123"
 */
export async function createTask(input: CreateTaskInput): Promise<Task> {
  // ...
}
```

### OpenAPI / Swagger for REST APIs

```yaml
paths:
  /api/tasks:
    post:
      summary: Create a task
      requestBody:
        required: true
        content:
          application/json:
            schema:
              $ref: '#/components/schemas/CreateTaskInput'
      responses:
        '201':
          description: Task created
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                $ref: '#/components/schemas/Task'
        '422':
          description: Validation error
```

## README Structure

Every project should have a README that covers:

```markdown
# Project Name

One-paragraph description of what this project does.

## Quick Start
1. Clone the repo
2. Install dependencies: `npm install`
3. Set up environment: `cp .env.example .env`
4. Run the dev server: `npm run dev`

## Commands
| Command | Description |
|---------|-------------|
| `npm run dev` | Start development server |
| `npm test` | Run tests |
| `npm run build` | Production build |
| `npm run lint` | Run linter |

## Architecture
Brief overview of the project structure and key design decisions.
Link to ADRs for details.

## Contributing
How to contribute, coding standards, PR process.
```

## Changelog Maintenance

For shipped features:

```markdown
# Changelog

## [1.2.0] - 2025-01-20
### Added
- Task sharing: users can share tasks with team members (#123)
- Email notifications for task assignments (#124)

### Fixed
- Duplicate tasks appearing when rapidly clicking create button (#125)

- Task list now loads 50 items per page (was 20) for better UX (#126)
```

## Documentation for Agents

Special consideration for AI agent context:

- **CLAUDE.md / rules files** — Document project conventions so agents follow them
- **Spec files** — Keep specs updated so agents build the right thing
- **ADRs** — Help agents understand why past decisions were made (prevents re-deciding)
- **Inline gotchas** — Prevent agents from falling into known traps

## Prose Review

After checking the technical content, review the prose for the people who will use it. Clearer wording must not change the decision or its limits.

1. Mark the details that must survive the edit: names, numbers and units, commands, paths, links, conditions, trade-offs, and uncertainty. Check them against the available code and decision context; flag anything you cannot substantiate.
2. Replace stock introductions, promotional adjectives, and repeated summaries with the concrete information the reader needs. Do not replace an unsupported claim with an invented example or a stronger guarantee. Keep necessary technical repetition and the project's established terminology.
3. Compare the edited document with the original and its sources. Restore any lost qualifier or caveat, verify command and code examples still work as documented, and explain any unresolved factual question rather than polishi

[NODE 5607]
rs.** Order findings by leverage: correctness and security first, then structural regressions and missed simplifications, then everything else. Don't bury a real issue under cosmetic nits — a few high-conviction comments beat a long list. If you have one structural problem and ten nits, the structural problem *is* the review.

### Step 5: Verify the Verification

Check the author's verification story:

```
- What tests were run?
- Did the build pass?
- Was the change tested manually?
- Are there screenshots for UI changes?
- Is there a before/after comparison?
```

## Multi-Model Review Pattern

Use different models for different review perspectives:

```
Model A writes the code
    │
    ▼
Model B reviews for correctness and architecture
    │
    ▼
Model A addresses the feedback
    │
    ▼
Human makes the final call
```

This catches issues that a single model might miss — different models have different blind spots.

**Example prompt for a review agent:**
```
Review this code change for correctness, security, and adherence to
our project conventions. The spec says [X]. The change should [Y].
Flag any issues as Critical, Required, Optional, or Nit.
```

## Dead Code Hygiene

After any refactoring or implementation change, check for orphaned code:

1. Identify code that is now unreachable or unused
2. List it explicitly
3. **Ask before deleting:** "Should I remove these now-unused elements: [list]?"

Don't leave dead code lying around — it confuses future readers and agents. But don't silently delete things you're not sure about. When in doubt, ask.

```
DEAD CODE IDENTIFIED:
- formatLegacyDate() in src/utils/date.ts — replaced by formatDate()
- OldTaskCard component in src/components/ — replaced by TaskCard
- LEGACY_API_URL constant in src/config.ts — no remaining references
→ Safe to remove these?
```

## Review Speed

Slow reviews block entire teams. The cost of context-switching to review is less than the waiting cost imposed on others.

- **Respond within one business day** — this is the maximum, not the target
- **Ideal cadence:** Respond shortly after a review request arrives, unless deep in focused coding. A typical change should complete multiple review rounds in a single day
- **Prioritize fast individual responses** over quick final approval. Quick feedback reduces frustration even if multiple rounds are needed
- **Large changes:** Ask the author to split them rather than reviewing one massive changeset

## Handling Disagreements

When resolving review disputes, apply this hierarchy:

1. **Technical facts and data** override opinions and preferences
2. **Style guides** are the absolute authority on style matters
3. **Software design** must be evaluated on engineering principles, not personal preference
4. **Codebase consistency** is acceptable if it doesn't degrade overall health

**Don't accept "I'll clean it up later."** Experience shows deferred cleanup rarely happens. Require cleanup before submission unless it's a genuine emergency. If surrounding issues can't be addressed in this change, require filing a bug with self-assignment.

## Honesty in Review

When reviewing code — whether written by you, another agent, or a human:

- **Don't rubber-stamp.** "LGTM" without evidence of review helps no one.
- **Don't soften real issues.** "This might be a minor concern" when it's a bug that will hit production is dishonest.
- **Quantify problems when possible.** "This N+1 query will add ~50ms per item in the list" is better than "this could be slow."
- **Push back on approaches with clear problems.** Sycophancy is a failure mode in reviews. If the implementation has issues, say so directly and propose alternatives.
- **Accept override gracefully.** If the author has full context and disagrees, defer to their judgment. Comment on code, not people — reframe personal critiques to focus on the code itself.

## Dependency Discipline

Part of code review is dependency review:

**Before adding any dependency:**
1. Does the existing stack solve this? (Often it does.)
2. How large is the dependency? (Check bundle impact.)
3. Is it actively maintained? (Check last commit, open issues.)
4. Does it have known vulnerabilities? (`npm audit`)
5. What's the license? (Must be compatible with the project.)

**Rule:** Prefer standard library and existing utilities over new dependencies. Every dependency is a liability.

**Upgrading an existing dependency** is a code change like any other, and the riskiest upgrades are the ones merged in bulk with a message like "bump deps." Review them with the same discipline:

1. **Read the changelog, not just the version number.** Semver is a promise the maintainer may not have kept — a "patch" can carry a behavioral change. For a major bump, read the migration notes and find what breaks.
2. **One dependency per change.** Upgrade and merge them individually (or in small related groups). When a bulk bump breaks the build, you've lost which package did it; a single-package change makes the cause obvious and the revert clean.
3. **Let the tests decide.** The upgrade is verified by a green suite before *and* after, not by "it installed." If coverage around the dependency's behavior is thin, that gap is the real finding — add a test first.
4. **Mind the transitive graph.** Most installed packages are ones nobody chose directly. Review the lockfile diff, not just `package.json`; a single direct bump can pull in dozens of indirect changes.
5. **Keep the lockfile honest.** Commit it, review its diff, and never hand-edit it. The lockfile is the thing that actually pins what ships.

For triaging `npm audit` findings and supply-chain risk (typosquatting, compromised maintainers), follow the `security-and-hardening` skill — this section covers the upgrade *workflow*, that one covers the security verdict.

## The Review Checklist

```markdown
## Review: [PR/Change title]

### Context
- [ ] I understand what this change does and why

### Correctness
- [ ] Change matches spec/task requirements
- [ ] Edge cases handled
- [ ] Error paths handled
- [ ] Tests cover the change adequately

### Readability
- [ ] Names are clear and consistent
- [ ] Logic is straightforward
- [ ] No unnecessary complexity

### Architecture
- [ ] Follows existing patterns
- [ ] No unnecessary coupling or dependencies
- [ ] Appropriate abstraction level
- [ ] Refactors reduce complexity rather than relocate it
- [ ] No feature logic in shared modules; file stays within a healthy size

### Security
- [ ] No secrets in code
- [ ] Input validated at boundaries
- [ ] No injection vulnerabilities
- [ ] Auth checks in place
- [ ] External data sources treated as untrusted

### Performance
- [ ] No N+1 patterns
- [ ] No unbounded operations
- [ ] Pagination on list endpoints

### Verification
- [ ] Tests pass
- [ ] Build succeeds
- [ ] Manual verification done (if applicable)

### Verdict
- [ ] **Approve** — Ready to merge
- [ ] **Request changes** — Issues must be addressed
```

## Common Rationalizations

| Rationalization | Reality |
|---|---|
| "It works, that's good enough" | Working code that's unreadable, insecure, or architecturally wrong creates debt that compounds. |
| "I wrote it, so I know it's correct" | Authors are blind to their own assumptions. Every change benefits from another set of eyes. |
| "We'll clean it up later" | Later never comes. The review is the quality gate — use it. Require cleanup before merge, not after. |
| "AI-generated code is probably fine" | AI code needs more scrutiny, not less. It's confident and plausible, even when wrong. |
| "The tests pass, so it's good" | Tests are necessary but not sufficient. They don't catch architecture problems, security issues, or readability concerns. |
| "The refactor makes it cleaner" | Relocating complexity isn't reducing it. If the reader still holds the same number of concepts, the structure didn't improve — look for the version where branches disappear. |
| "It's only a small addition to this file" | Small diffs still push files past a healthy size and bolt branches onto unrelated flows. Judge the resulting structure, not the diff size. |
| "It's just a version bump" | A bump is a behavior change you didn't write. Read the changelog; semver doesn't guarantee no breakage. |
| "I'll upgrade everything in one PR to save time" | A bulk bump that breaks the build hides which package did it. One dependency per change keeps the cause and the revert clean. |

## Red Flags

- PRs merged without any review
- Review that only checks if tests pass (ignoring other axes)
- "LGTM" without evidence of actual review
- Security-sensitive changes without security-focused review
- Large PRs that are "too big to review properly" (split them)
- No regression tests with bug fix PRs
- Review comments without severity labels — makes it unclear what's required vs optional
- Accepting "I'll fix it later" — it never happens
- A refactor that moves code around without reducing the number of concepts a reader must hold
- A change that grows an already-large file instead of decomposing it
- New conditionals scattered into unrelated code paths (a missing abstraction)
- A bespoke helper that duplicates an existing canonical one, or feature logic placed in a shared module
- A bulk "bump dependencies" PR with no changelog review and no per-package isolation
- A lockfile change that's hand-edited, uncommitted, or merged without reviewing its diff

After review is complete:

- [ ] All Critical issues are resolved
- [ ] All Required (no-prefix) changes are resolved or explicitly deferred with justification
- [ ] Tests pass
- [ ] Build succeeds
- [ ] The verification story is documented (what changed, how it was verified)
- [ ] Dependency upgrades were reviewed against their changelog, is

## Folder 1 — SQLite/NetBeans Swing payroll manager

**Location:** `1/-/src/EmployeePayrollMph/`. There are 12 Java source files, many NetBeans `.form` files, images and bundled JARs. `build/classes/` also contains compiled `.class` files and form copies; those are build output, not a second source implementation. The project metadata names `EmployeePayrollMph.EmployeePayrollMph` as its entry point.

**How it works:** the entry frame presents a login form. Its handler queries the SQLite `Users` table using a prepared statement, stores the selected user's ID/name in static fields on `Emp`, records a login event in `EmployeeAudit`, then opens `MainMenu`. The menu opens employee management, allowances, salary update, deductions, payment records, search and audit. The included SQLite database schema has `Employee_info`, `Users`, `Allowance`, `Salary_Deduction`, and `EmployeeAudit` tables.

The `Employee` frame performs employee add/update/delete against `Employee_info`, including an image BLOB. `Allowance` reads an employee, calculates an allowance total, and inserts a row into `Allowance`. `SalaryDeductions` inserts a deduction record. `EmployeeSalary` looks up the employee plus stored allowances/deductions to prepare a payslip; the app bundles iText, and the menu has PDF report export handlers. This is therefore more of a database-backed admin CRUD app than a clean payroll-calculation library.

**Caveats:** the SQLite connector uses a hard-coded Windows path under one developer's `C:\Users\...` directory even though database files are included in the project. Several screens are mainly generated Swing code; `EmployeeAttendance` and `EmployeeLeave` exist, but their presence alone does not establish a complete persisted attendance/leave workflow. The login's role check uses Java string identity (`==`) and contains an empty `if (count == 1);` statement, so the code should not be treated as a reliable authentication example without checking/fixing that flow.

**Course connection:** the code is useful for seeing Swing event handlers, JDBC/SQLite, CRUD and report generation. There is no source evidence tying it to CP1, CP2, MS1 or MS2, so I would not label it as your coursework baseline.

## Folders 2 and 5 — one Swing/MySQL app under two different labels

**Locations:** `2/-/` and `5/-/`. Each has 49 Java files, many NetBeans `.form` layouts and image assets, a Maven file, and two third-party time-picker JARs. The active entry point is `main.main`, which opens `Jframes.LogInNew`; `Archived/` contains four older screens.

**How it works:** the login screen queries the local MySQL `user_accounts` table and routes Admin/IT users to `AdminHomeDashboard`, other users to `HomeDashboard`. The employee dashboard links to profile, salary, attendance, leave requests and overtime requests. The admin side links to employee records, salary/attendance, accounts, leave approvals and overtime approvals. The screens issue SQL directly through `Classes.db`, which connects to a local MySQL database named `motorph`. SQL references tables named `employees`, `user_accounts`, `attendance_records`, `salary`, `leave_requests`, and `overtime_requests`.

There is a `Classes/` package with `Employee`, `Salary`, `Attendance`, `Deduction`, `Payroll`, `UserAuthentication`, `Admin`, `HR`, `Manager`, request and task classes. These communicate the intended domain model, but multiple methods are empty placeholders (for example, model-level payroll/CRUD methods). The working behavior is mostly in Swing-frame event handlers. Salary computation logic appears in both `CreateSalary` and `UpdateSalaryAdmin`, which each query attendance and calculate salary/deductions. This is an example of a GUI-heavy project with some OOP-shaped classes, not a fully separated model/service architecture.

**Important duplication finding:** folders 2 and 5 are not two materially different codebases. A recursive comparison found only four differences: `.DS_Store`, `README.md`, and author-comment lines in `Classes/Employee.java` and `main/main.java`. The executable Java logic, forms, assets and build file otherwise match. Folder 5's README labels it MO-IT103 H1101 Group 1 / CP2; folder 2's README labels it MO-IT110 H2101 Group 3 / OOP. That makes them different submission *packagings/labels*, but essentially the same program. The folder 2 label does not by itself demonstrate that this is your approved MS1 design or your authored work.

**Caveats:** the MySQL schema/setup is not included as a self-contained database export; running requires a local `motorph` database and compatible account setup. Some domain-layer methods are stubs, while substantial behavior is coupled to the UI. The credentials are database-backed, but the source uses direct password comparison; this is not a security design to copy.

**Course connection:** folder 5 is explicitly CP2. Folder 2 is labelled MO-IT110 OOP, but the repository does not include an MS1 design package connecting these classes to an approved design. Treat it as a CP2-style app/OOP comparison unless the mentor confirms more.

## Folder 3 — small CP1/terminal-assessment console exercises

**Location:** `3/-/`. The README identifies a COMPROG1 A1101 Terminal Assessment submission and describes a Phase 1 console payroll system. There are seven Java files, employee CSV/TXT samples, and NetBeans metadata. Six Java files are in package `motorph`; `MotorPH_ReadFromFile.java` is in the default package, so it is a separate runnable entry point.

**How it works:** the files are small, independent demonstrations rather than one integrated app. They show fixed-value examples for hours worked, gross pay and semi-monthly salary; a separate class calculates example deductions; the file-reader program opens `employee_data.csv`, reads salary from a fixed column, applies its own sample deductions, and prints a result. `ComputeGrossPay` has a reusable static multiplication method, while the other examples largely hard-code the employee/time/pay inputs in `main`.

**Caveats:** the README describes a longer planned progression, but the source is still a set of small console programs, not a GUI, database-backed system or connected payroll architecture. The deduction rates differ between files and are explicitly example-style flat rates; they are not a safe source for official payroll rules. The folder's named author is not evidence that the current user authored it.

**Course connection:** this is the clearest CP1/procedural foundation in the numbered set: variables, arithmetic, conditions, methods and basic file reading. It is not evidence of a personal CP2 app. Given the user's CP1-to-OOP path, this may be useful as a prior-learning comparison, but do not describe it as their submission without confirmation.

## Folder 4 — layered CP2 Swing/CSV payroll app

**Location:** `4/-/`. It has 50 Java files: 42 under `src/main/java/com/motorph/` and 8 under `src/test/java/com/motorph/`, plus CSV inputs, images, Maven metadata and VS Code settings. `sources.txt` contains Windows paths naming a `CP2_GROUP-4` project. There is no README explaining the feature set or assignment milestones.

**Structure and flow:** `Main.main()` starts the Swing login. On successful login, `initializeApplication()` constructs a `DataRepository`, loads employees and attendance, then wires `EmployeeService`, `PayrollService`, `ReportService` to their controllers and gives those controllers to `MainFrame`. The view is divided into dashboard, employee, payroll, reports and leave panels. The packages are `controller`, `service`, `model`, `repository`, `dao`, `security`, `leave`, `util` and `view` (including dialogs/renderers).

- `DataRepository` reads employee and attendance CSVs, parses dates/times and builds `Employee`/`AttendanceRecord` objects.
- `EmployeeService` searches and manages employee records and writes employee changes back to CSV; attendance lookup is exposed by date/range methods.
- `PayrollService` selects an employee and period, builds a `PaySlip`, and can generate payroll for all employees. `PayrollProcessor` supplies gross-pay, SSS-table, PhilHealth, Pag-IBIG and withholding-tax calculations. `ReportService` builds payslip and weekly/monthly summaries.
- Controllers validate request parameters and delegate to services; Swing panels call controllers.
- The CSV files contain employee details, attendance records and user credentials. The bundled sample files have 35 employee data rows and 5,168 attendance rows (excluding headers); the runtime probe loaded 35 employee rows.

**Caveats:** the repo mixes a reasonably separated architecture with helper/demo code (`EmployeeDAO`, CSV tests and test utilities) that is not obviously part of the main wiring. The leave request classes/panel exist, but the startup wiring shown in `Main` does not construct a `LeaveRequestService` or pass it into the frame. Several test classes are standalone/manual `main` programs, and some use hard-coded Windows paths; the presence of JUnit in the Maven file does not mean the available checks are all JUnit tests. Payroll formulas still need validation against the current approved specification, not merely against code in another folder.

**Course connection:** useful as a CP2 example of Swing + CSV and of separating controllers/services/models/repositories. The course identity is inferred from the source path, not stated in an official README; there is no explicit MS1/MS2 linkage.

## Folder 6 — explicit MO-IT110 MS2 refactor example

**Location:** `6/-/`. Its README names MO-IT110 OOP Milestone 2 and says the project refactors a CP2 Java Swing app into an approved MS1 design. It has 22 production Java files under `src/motorph/`, 10 plain-Java tests under `test/motorph/`, CSV data, CP2 reference outputs, NetBeans metadata and an Ant build file. The declared main class is `motorph.MotorPH`.

**Structure and flow:** `MotorPH` opens `LoginFrame`. UI classes are under `ui/`; the payroll domain is separated into `model/`, `deduction/`, `service/` and `user/`.

1. `CSVDataHandler` loads employees and attendance from CSV and creates model objects.
2. `Employee` is an abstract class; `RegularEmployee` and `ProbationaryEmployee` supply subtype behavior such as allowances.
3. `AttendanceRecord` calculates hours/cutoff membership.
4. `PayrollProcessor` accepts a list of `Deduction` objects (SSS, PhilHealth, Pag-IBIG and tax), totals cutoff hours, calculates gross/deductions/net, and creates an immutable `Payslip`.
5. UI frames display employee/payroll results and save payroll CSV output.
6. `User`, `EmployeeUser` and `PayrollStaff` demonstrate authentication/role permissions for the employee-lookup vs staff screens.

The README says the implementation preserves CP2's cutoff behavior and describes how it rounds money, applies deductions and lists allowances. It also cautions that the salary tables/rules were carried from CP2 rather than independently verified against a current MotorPH/government specification. The README reports 167 checks and 0 failures, with CP2 comparison differences on 3 of 476 rows; those are project-reported results, not runs performed in this review.

**Course connection:** direct MS2 relevance by its own README; the code is a concrete example of implementing an approved design, using encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism and a view/backend split. The CP2 source commit and authorship/permission should be confirmed before adopting any code or presenting it as the user's work.

## Folder 7 — Swing/CSV payroll app with unclear submission identity

**Location:** `7/-/src/motorphpayrollsystem/`. There are 35 Java files, NetBeans forms/assets, and bundled OpenCSV, Commons Lang and AbsoluteLayout libraries. There is no README, no course/team label, and no CSV data file in the folder. The project main class is `MotorPHPayrollSystem`.

**Structure and flow:** the main class tries to create `attendance.csv`, loads employee data through `EmployeeData`, and opens `loginUI`. Login looks up an employee row in a CSV and compares a password against column 20. On success it opens `DashboardUI`. `EmployeeData` keeps the CSV rows in a static shared list and offers add/update/delete/profile methods that rewrite the CSV. The UI includes employee dashboard/profile, attendance clock-in/clock-out and history, employee records, admin employee add/update/delete, payroll screens and a bulk-payroll/export screen. `Attendance` and `CSVUtil` provide CSV persistence; `Payroll`, `ContributionCalculator`, `PayrollCalculator` and `PayrollProcessor` contain pay logic; `FullTimeEmployee`/`PartTimeEmployee` and `EmployeeMapper` provide model objects.

**What is only partial or unclear:** `MotorPH_Employee Data.csv`, required by `EmployeeData`, is not included. Attendance data is created as an empty CSV when absent. `LeaveRequest` and `OvertimeRequest` are domain classes, but a search shows no leave-request workflow in the screens; the overtime request model is stored on the processor but not used by its main processing method. The payroll processor's comments describe overtime as a temporary/unfinished path. So the classes indicate intended scope, not proof every listed capability is operational.

**Course connection:** its class hierarchy and UI/backend concepts could be compared to OOP course topics, but no source evidence ties it to a particular MO-IT110 module, MS1 design or user's own submission. It is not self-contained enough to treat as a runnable reference without its expected employee CSV.

<h3 align="center">
  Foodya is a full-featured <b>Restaurant POS (Point of Sale) system</b> coupled with a simple website. It is designed to help restaurants manage their day-to-day operations efficiently, including orders, tables, menu items, bookings, employees, transactions, and reports. The system includes <b>Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)</b> per page to manage permissions for different users.
</h3>

<p align="center">
    <a href="#"> Documentation </a>·
    <a href="https://mail.google.com/mail/?view=cm&fs=1&to=shahzaibawan1357@gmail.com"> Request Feature </a>·
    <a href="https://www.linkedin.com/in/shahzaib-awan-dev/">Connect on Linkedin</a>
</p>

---

## 🚀 Features

### User & Access Management

- Manage users: add, update, deactivate/activate.
- Manage roles: create multiple roles with specific permissions.
- Manage modules/pages: control access to each page in the app.
- Assign permissions: customize access per role for different pages.

### Menu & Orders

- Menu Categories: create, update, delete multiple categories.
- Menu Items: manage items with variants and sizes.
- Orders: handle Dine-in, Take-away, and Drive-thru orders.
  - Dine-in orders: select tables, place/reselect orders, fetch existing orders.
- Bookings: manage table bookings with optional advance payment.
- Invoices: view, print, and track past invoices and order details.

### Employee & Salary Management

- Employee management: add employees, manage designations and promotions.
- Salary management:
  - Update salaries, track changes over time.
  - Generate monthly salaries with one click.
  - Track payment status: Pending, Paid.
  - Include bonus, penalties, and custom reasons.
  - Print salary statements and history.

### Transactions & Finances

- Manage transaction categories (salaries, invoices, others).
- Add manual income and expenses.
- Reports:
  - Summary cards: monthly income, expense, active employees, total employees.
  - Charts: visualize monthly/yearly profit and expense trends.
  - Hover cards: view transaction details on hover.

### Analytics & Visualizations

- Charts for financial analysis using **Chart.js** and **Recharts**.
- Animated website elements with **GSAP** for smooth user experience.

---

## 🛠 Tech Stack

### 🎨 Frontend

- **Next.js 15 (App Router)** – React framework for server-side rendering and routing.
- **React Hook Form** – Efficient form handling.
- **ShadCN UI & Cult UI** – Prebuilt, customizable UI components.
- **Tailwind CSS** – Utility-first styling.
- **GSAP** – Animations for website interactions.
- **useSWR** – Data fetching with caching and revalidation.

### 🗄️ Backend & Database

- **TypeScript** – Strongly typed codebase.
- **Drizzle ORM** – Type-safe ORM for MySQL.
- **MySQL** – Relational database for structured data.
- **Auth.js (Credentials-based)** – Secure authentication.
- **Zod** – Input validation and schema enforcement.

### 🧰 Utilities & Libraries

- **Chart.js & Recharts** – Data visualization.
- **React Hot Toast** – Notifications.
- **ExcelJS & jsPDF** – Export data to Excel or PDF.
- **SWR** – Data fetching and caching.
- **Radix UI Components** – Accessible UI elements.
- **clsx & tailwind-merge** – Dynamic class management.

## 📦 Installation

```bash
# 1. Clone the repo
git clone https://github.com/CodifyCanvas/foodya.git
cd foodya

# 2. Install dependencies
npm install

# 3. Set up .env file
cp .env
# Fill in your DATABASE_URL, AUTH_SECRET, etc.

# 4. Run Drizzle migrations
npx drizzle-kit push

# 5. Run dev server
npm run dev

# 6. Build for Production
npm run build

# 7. Start Server
npm start
```

namespace App\Http\Controllers;

use App\Payroll;
use App\Employee;
use App\Role;
use Session;
use Paginate;
use Illuminate\Http\Request;

class PayrollController extends Controller
{
     public function __construct()
    {
        $this->middleware('auth');
    }
    /**
     * Show the form for creating a new resource.
     *
     * @return \Illuminate\Http\Response
     */
    public function create($id){
        $employee = Employee::findOrFail($id);
		return view('payroll.create')->with('employee',$employee);
    }

    /**
     * Store a newly created resource in storage.
     *
     * @param  \Illuminate\Http\Request  $request
     * @return \Illuminate\Http\Response
     */
    public function store(Request $request, $id){
		
	   $this->validate($request,[
			'hours'=> 'required',
			'rate'=>'required',
			'over_time' => 'required|bool'
		]);
		
	    $payroll = Payroll::create([
			'hours' => $request->hours,
			'rate' => $request->rate,
			'over_time' => $request->over_time,
			'employee_id' => $id
		]);
		
		$payroll->grossPay();
		$payroll->save();
		
		Session::flash('success', 'Payroll Created');
		return redirect()->route('payrolls.show',['id'=>$id]);	
    }

    /**
     * Display the specified resource.
     *
     * @param  int  $id
     * @return \Illuminate\Http\Response
     */
    public function payrollIndex($id){
		$employee = Employee::findOrFail($id);
        return view('payroll.payroll')->with('employee',$employee);
    }

    /**
     * Show the form for editing the specified resource.
     *
     * @param  int  $id
     * @return \Illuminate\Http\Response
     */
    public function edit($id){
        $payroll = Payroll::findOrFail($id);
		return view('payroll.edit')->with('payroll',$payroll);
    }

    /**
     * Update the specified resource in storage.
     *
     * @param  \Illuminate\Http\Request  $request
     * @param  int  $id
     * @return \Illuminate\Http\Response
     */
    public function update(Request $request, $id)
    {
        $this->validate($request,[
			'hours'=> 'required',
			'rate'=>'required',
			'over_time' => 'required|bool'
		]);
		
		$payroll = Payroll::findOrFail($id);
		$payroll->hours = $request->hours;
		$payroll->rate= $request->rate;
		$payroll->over_time = $request->over_time;
		$payroll->save();		
		
		$payroll->grossPay();
		$payroll->save();
		
		Session::flash('success', 'Payroll Updated ready for download');
		return redirect()->route('payrolls.show',['id'=>$payroll->employee_id]);			
    }

    /**
     * Remove the specified resource from storage.
     *
     * @param  int  $id
     * @return \Illuminate\Http\Response
     */
    public function destroy($id)
    {
        $payroll=Payroll::findOrFail($id);
		$payroll->delete();
		
		Session::flash('success','Payroll Deleted');
		return redirect()->back();
    }
	public function bin(){
		$payrolls=Payroll::onlyTrashed()->get();
		return view('payroll.bin')->with('payrolls', $payrolls);
	}
	
	public function restore($id){
		$payroll=Payroll::withTrashed()->where('id', $id)->first();
		$payroll->restore();
		
		Session::flash('success', 'payroll row is restored.');
		return redirect()->route('employees.index');
	}
	
	public function kill($id){
		$payroll=Payroll::withTrashed()->where('id', $id)->first();		
		$payroll->forceDelete();
		
		Session::flash('success', 'payroll permanently destroyed.');
		return redirect()->route('employees.index');
	}
}
<?php

namespace App;

use Illuminate\Database\Eloquent\Model;
use Illuminate\Database\Eloquent\SoftDeletes;

class Payroll extends Model
{
    use SoftDeletes;
	
	protected $dates = ['deleted_at'];
	
	protected $fillable=['employee_id','over_time','hours','rate','total'];
	
	
	public function employee(){
		return $this->belongsTo('App\Employee');
	}
	
	public function grossPay(){
		$calc = 0;
		if($this->employee->full_time && !$this->over_time){
			return $this->gross = $this->employee->role->salary;
		}
		if($this->employee->full_time && $this->over_time){
			$calc = $this->hours * $this->rate;
			return $this->gross = $calc + $this->employee->role->salary;
		}
		if($this->over_time || !$this->full_time){
			$calc = $this->hours * $this->rate;
			return $this->gross = $calc;
		}
		return $this->gross = 0;
	}
	
	
}

namespace App;

		'street','town','city','country'];
	
	public $with = ['role','payrolls'];
	
	public function role(){
		return $this->belongsTo('App\Role');
	}
	
	public function payrolls(){
		return $this->hasMany('App\Payroll');
	}
	
	
}
