1. Introduction MotorPH has relied on fragmented manual processes, such as paper timecards, spreadsheet-based payroll calculations, and branch-speciﬁc data reconciliation, to drive its growing workforce across multiple locations, which led to delayed payslips, calculation errors, and general bottlenecks that draw out the series of processes caused through repetition due to minor revisions in the payroll. The MotorPH Payroll System is designed to simplify and automate the once convoluted end-to-end payroll process for MotorPH, encompassing attendance tracking, salary computation, leave management, and compliance to government contributions. Driven by the shortcomings identiﬁed in the Business Requirement Speciﬁcation (BRS) and the Current State Assessment of existing manual workﬂows, the system addresses inefﬁciencies, reduces processing times, and enhances data accuracy. 1.1. Purpose This document provides a detailed description of how the MotorPH Payroll System and its components function and interact, serving as the basis and blueprint for the development, implementation, and maintenance of the said system. 1.2. Scope The MotorPH Payroll System is designed to support the core administrative processes essential to compensating employees accurately, securely, and on time, primarily covering the digital management of employee records, attendance tracking through both remote and on-site channels, and the smoother handling of payroll computations, deductions, and reporting, whilst also accommodating for basic leave coordination and internal communication surrounding payroll-related matters, all within a secure, role-aware environment that respects data sensitivity and organisational hierarchy. Database Overview The MotorPH Payroll System database is built in a way to allow users to automate, organise, and streamline MotorPH payroll processes systematically to provide the prerogative of having minimal struggle in handling the payroll operations so that users may allocate efforts unto more substantially demanding tasks. Through the centralisation of most payroll-related data into a singular, secure, and scalable repository, the system facilitates rapid data retrieval and processing, which becomes indispensable for timely salary computations, tax management, and adherence to legal contributions and compliance. Thus, for this instance, we deliver an expectation that this database will not just bring about changes in improvement with data derivation and the alleviation of unnecessary exertion but also an effective means through which future growth of the organisation may be faci

--- p24: Relationship Cardinality Foreign Keys Purpose Employee -> Address 1:1 (Employee - addressID) Each employee is assigned an address. Employee -> Position N:1 (Employee - positionID) Every employee holds a speciﬁc position. Employee -> Supervisor N:1 (Employee - supervisorID) References the supervisor of the employee. Address -> Cities N:1 (Address - cityID) Each address entry is located within a speciﬁc city. Position -> Department N:1 (Position - departmentID) Positions are assigned within departments. Supervisor -> Employee 1:1 (Supervisor - employeeID) Supervisors are employees themselves, connecting both tables directly. Schedule -> Employee 1:1 (Schedule - employeeID) Each employee is assigned a schedule. Changelog -> Employee N:1 (Changelog - employeeID) Tracks changes made by the employee. LeaveBalance -> Leave Type N:1 (LeaveBalance - leaveType) Indicates the leave type applicable

[NODE 11497]

    private void handleEmployees(HttpExchange exchange) throws IOException {

        String method = exchange.getRequestMethod();

            if ("GET".equals(method)) {
                RequestServices services = servicesFor(exchange);
                if ("/api/employees".equals(path) || "/api/employees/".equals(path)) {
                    String query = queryParameter(exchange.getRequestURI().getRawQuery(), "q");
                    List<Employee> matches = services.employeeService.searchEmployees(query);
                    int total = services.employeeService.listEmployees().size();
                    sendJson(exchange, 200, employeesToJson(matches, total));
                    return;
                }
                if (!path.startsWith("/api/employees/")) {
                    sendJson(exchange, 404, "{\"error\":\"Employee not found\"}");
                    return;
                }
                String id = path.substring("/api/employees/".length());
                if (id.isEmpty() || id.contains("/")) {
                    sendJson(exchange, 404, "{\"error\":\"Employee not found\"}");
                    return;
                }
                Optional<Employee> employee = services.employeeService.findEmployee(id);
                if (!employee.isPresent()) {
                    sendJson(exchange, 404, "{\"error\":\"Employee not found\"}");
                    return;
                }
                sendJson(exchange, 200, "{\"item\":" + employeeToJson(employee.get()) + "}");
                return;
            }

package ph.motorph.web;

import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.util.Objects;

/** A directory record: identity, placement and the pay inputs MotorPH's payslip needs. */
public final class Employee {
    private final String id;
    private final String name;
    private final String department;
    private final String role;
    private final String location;
    private final String status;
    private final BigDecimal monthlyBasic;
    private final BigDecimal riceSubsidy;
    private final BigDecimal phoneAllowance;
    private final BigDecimal clothingAllowance;

    /** Directory-only record with no pay data; used where salary is irrelevant. */
    public Employee(String id, String name, String department, String role, String location, String status) {
        this(id, name, department, role, location, status, null, null, null, null);
    }

    public Employee(String id, String name, String department, String role, String location, String status,
                    BigDecimal monthlyBasic, BigDecimal riceSubsidy, BigDecimal phoneAllowance, BigDecimal clothingAllowance) {
        this.id = requireText(id, "id");
        this.name = requireText(name, "name");
        this.department = requireText(department, "department");
        this.role = requireText(role, "role");
        this.location = requireText(location, "location");
        this.status = requireText(status, "status");
        this.monthlyBasic = nonNegative(monthlyBasic, "Monthly basic pay");
        this.riceSubsidy = nonNegative(riceSubsidy, "Rice subsidy");
        this.phoneAllowance = nonNegative(phoneAllowance, "Phone allowance");
        this.clothingAllowance = nonNegative(clothingAllowance, "Clothing allowance");
    }

    /** MotorPH numbers employees with five digits; anything else is not a directory ID. */
    public static boolean isValidEmployeeNumber(String id) {
        return id != null && id.matches("[0-9]{5}");
    }

    public Employee withPay(BigDecimal basic, BigDecimal rice, BigDecimal phone, BigDecimal clothing) {
        return new Employee(id, name, department, role, location, status, basic, rice, phone, clothing);
    }

def main() -> None:
    rows = list(csv.DictReader(CSV.open(encoding="utf-8-sig")))
    lines = []
    for row in rows:
        emp_id = row["Employee #"].strip()
        name = f'{row["First Name"].strip()} {row["Last Name"].strip()}'
        position = row["Position"].strip()
        dept = department_for(position)
        location = row["Address"].strip() or "Quezon City"
        # The CSV's own Status column holds employment type (Regular/Probationary),
        # not the Active/On leave state this model needs. Everyone is Active.
        status = "Active"
        basic = money(row["Basic Salary"])
        rice = money(row["Rice Subsidy"])
        phone = money(row["Phone Allowance"])
        cloth = money(row["Clothing Allowance"])

            f'        addFixture(new Employee("{emp_id}", "{name}", "{dept}", '
            f'"{position}", "{location}", "{status}",\n'

/**
 * Saved payroll runs under users/{uid}/demoPayrollRuns/{runId}. Each run stores its header,
 * the ruleset version, the calculation assumptions, and every resulting payslip line, so a
 * stored run can be re-read without recomputing or re-deriving policy.
 */
public final class FirestorePayrollStore implements PayrollStore {
    private static final String COLLECTION = "demoPayrollRuns";
    private final FirestoreRestClient client;

    public FirestorePayrollStore(FirestoreRestClient client) {
        if (client == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("client must not be null");
        this.client = client;
    }

    @Override
    public List<PayrollRun> findAll() {
        List<PayrollRun> runs = new ArrayList<>();
        for (JsonObject document : client.listDocuments(client.userCollection(COLLECTION))) {
            runs.add(fromDocument(document));
        }
        runs.sort((a, b) -> b.createdAt().compareTo(a.createdAt()));
        return runs;
    }

    public Optional<PayrollRun> findById(String id) {
        if (id == null) return Optional.empty();

private void handlePayroll(HttpExchange exchange) throws IOException {
        String path = exchange.getRequestURI().getPath();
        String method = exchange.getRequestMethod();
        try {
            if ("GET".equals(method) && "/api/payroll/rules".equals(path)) {
                int year = parseIntYear(queryParameter(exchange.getRequestURI().getRawQuery(), "year"));
                PayrollRuleset ruleset = PayrollRuleset.forYear(year);
                sendJson(exchange, 200, rulesetToJson(ruleset));
                return;
            }
            if ("GET".equals(method) && "/api/payroll/timesheet".equals(path)) {
                String employeeId = queryParameter(exchange.getRequestURI().getRawQuery(), "employeeId");
                if (employeeId == null || employeeId.trim().isEmpty()) {
                    sendJson(exchange, 400, "{\"error\":\"employeeId is required\"}");
                    return;
                }
                RequestServices services = servicesFor(exchange);
                AttendanceService attendance = new AttendanceService(services.employeeService,
                    services.scheduleStore, services.attendanceStore);
                LocalDate from = parseOptionalDate(queryParameter(exchange.getRequestURI().getRawQuery(), "from"));
                LocalDate to = parseOptionalDate(queryParameter(exchange.getRequestURI().getRawQuery(), "to"));
                TimesheetService.Summary summary = new TimesheetService(attendance).summarise(employeeId, from, to);
                sendJson(exchange, 200, timesheetToJson(summary));
                return;
            }
            if ("POST".equals(method) && "/api/payroll/compare".equals(path)) {
                // Reference-only: our payslip is already computed above by PayrollService. This route
                // adds an independent second opinion and can never change the calculation.
                PayrollService.Input input = payrollInputFrom(readJsonBody(exchange));
                Payslip slip = new PayrollService().compute(input, PayrollRuleset.forYear(periodYear(input)));

    private static final PayrollRuleset Y2026 = new PayrollRuleset(2026);
    private static final PayrollRuleset Y2025 = new PayrollRuleset(2025);

    public static PayrollRuleset forYear(int year) {
        if (year == 2026) return Y2026;
        if (year == 2025) return Y2025;
        throw new IllegalArgumentException("No statutory ruleset is loaded for " + year
            + ". Available: 2025, 2026. Refusing to calculate outside a covered year.");
    }

[NODE 11854]
What all three agree on. Every one of them separates four things that our current code smashes
together:

[NODE 11855]
What none of them are. All three are customer support tools. They route an anonymous person's
problem to an agent. Ours is different in one decisive way: a payroll ticket is a request for a
change to a payroll record, and that change must be approved by a named person and then applied by
the engine. osTicket's "close the ticket" is not enough — we need "the ticket approved a ₱200 rice
subsidy increase, and payroll run PR-… applied it".

[NODE 11856]
So: copy the structure, not the purpose.

[NODE 11857]
From MO-IT108 §2.2.2 and the use-case diagram you sent, the tickets we need are:

[NODE 11858]
That is a different ticket per workflow, not one generic "issue". The use-case diagram shows
Tickets as a single use case with extension points — which is exactly the right model: one
table, a type column, and one handler per type.

  subject         free text, <= 120
  employeeId      who it is about (the requester may differ: HR raises a rate change for someone)
  requestedBy     who opened it
  queue           derived from type, never chosen by the client (§4.2)
  assigneeId      employee number of the handler, null until assigned
  status          OPEN | IN_PROGRESS | PENDING_APPROVAL | RESOLVED | CANCELLED

  createdAt / updatedAt / resolvedAt / resolvedBy

  entries[]       the conversation, append-only
    - type        MESSAGE (from the requester) | REPLY (public) | NOTE (internal only)
    - authorId, body, at

  events[]        the audit trail, append-only
    - what changed, from, to, by whom, when

package ph.motorph.web;

import java.util.Locale;

/**
 * The five account types named in MotorPH's System Design Document (MO-IT108 2nd Milestone,
 * §2.2.1 "RBAC Roles"). The order here is only display order; authority comes from {@link Policy}.
 */
public enum Role {
    SYSTEM_ADMIN("System Admin"),
    HR("HR"),
    PAYROLL("Payroll Staff"),
    SUPERVISOR("Supervisor"),
    EMPLOYEE("Employee");

    private final String label;

    Role(String label) {
        this.label = label;
    }

    public String label() {
        return label;
    }

    /**
     * Reads a role from an authority string. Anything unrecognised returns {@link #EMPLOYEE}, the
     * least-privileged role: an unknown or misspelled role can never grant access.
     */
    public static Role fromClaim(String value) {
        if (value == null) return EMPLOYEE;
        String key = value.trim().toUpperCase(Locale.ROOT).replace('-', '_').replace(' ', '_');
        switch (key) {
            case "SYSTEM_ADMIN":
            case "SYSTEMADMIN":
            case "ADMIN":
                return SYSTEM_ADMIN;
            case "HR":
            case "HR_MANAGEMENT":
                return HR;
            case "PAYROLL":
            case "PAYROLL_STAFF":
            case "PAYROLL_SUPERVISION":
                return PAYROLL;
            case "SUPERVISOR":
            case "SUPERVISOR_TEAM_LEAD":
            case "TEAM_LEAD":
                return SUPERVISOR;
            case "EMPLOYEE":
                return EMPLOYEE;
            default:
                return EMPLOYEE;
        }
    }
}

    private static String itemToJson(JsonObject item, String storage) {
        JsonObject response = new JsonObject();
        response.add("item", item);
        response.addProperty("storage", storage);
        return response.toString();
    }

    private static String workflowsToJson(List<DemoLeaveRequest> leaveRequests, List<DemoTicket> tickets, String storage) {
        JsonObject response = new JsonObject();
        JsonArray leaves = new JsonArray();
        for (DemoLeaveRequest request : leaveRequests) leaves.add(leaveToJson(request));
        JsonArray ticketItems = new JsonArray();
        for (DemoTicket ticket : tickets) ticketItems.add(ticketToJson(ticket));
        response.add("leaveRequests", leaves);
        response.add("tickets", ticketItems);
        response.addProperty("storage", storage);
        return response.toString();
    }

    private static JsonObject leaveToJson(DemoLeaveRequest request) {
        JsonObject item = new JsonObject();
        item.addProperty("id", request.getId());
        item.addProperty("employeeId", request.getEmployeeId());
        item.addProperty("employeeName", request.getEmployeeName());
        item.addProperty("leaveType", request.getLeaveType());
        item.addProperty("startDate", request.getStartDate());
        item.addProperty("endDate", request.getEndDate());
        item.addProperty("note", request.getNote());
        item.addProperty("status", request.getStatus());
        item.addProperty("submittedAt", request.getSubmittedAt());
        item.addProperty("cancelledAt", request.getCancelledAt());
        return item;
    }

    private static HttpResponse<String> postJson(URI uri, String json, String token, String uid) throws Exception {
        HttpRequest request = HttpRequest.newBuilder(uri).header("Accept", "application/json")
            .header("Content-Type", "application/json").header("Authorization", "Bearer " + token)
            .header("X-Firebase-UID", uid)
            .POST(HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.ofString(json, StandardCharsets.UTF_8)).build();
        return HTTP.send(request, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString(StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
    }

async function apiHeaders(extra = {}) {
  const headers = { Accept: 'application/json', ...extra };
  if (state.user) {
    const token = await state.user.getIdToken();
    headers.Authorization = `Bearer ${token}`;
    headers['X-Firebase-UID'] = state.user.uid;
  }
  return headers;
}

function freePort() {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    const server = net.createServer();
    server.once('error', reject);
    server.listen(0, '127.0.0.1', () => {
      const { port } = server.address();
      server.close(error => error ? reject(error) : resolve(port));
    });
  });
}

    stdio: ['ignore', 'pipe', 'pipe']
  });
  child.log = '';
  child.on('error', error => { child.log += `${label}: ${error.message}\n`; });

    stream.setEncoding('utf8');
    stream.on('data', chunk => { child.log = (child.log + chunk).slice(-8000); });

        item.addProperty("endDate", request.getEndDate());

        item.addProperty("status", request.getStatus());
        item.addProperty("submittedAt", request.getSubmittedAt());
        item.addProperty("cancelledAt", request.getCancelledAt());
        return item;
    }

    private void submitSalaryRate(HttpExchange exchange) throws IOException {
        JsonObject body = readJsonBody(exchange);
        String employeeId = requiredString(body, "employeeId");
        requireAccess(exchange, Policy.Entity.PAYROLL, Policy.Operation.UPDATE, employeeId);
        java.time.LocalDate effectiveFrom;
        try {
            effectiveFrom = java.time.LocalDate.parse(requiredString(body, "effectiveFrom"));
        } catch (DateTimeParseException ex) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("effectiveFrom must be a date like 2026-07-01.");
        }
        if (effectiveFrom.getDayOfMonth() != 1) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("A rate takes effect on the first day of a month, "
                + "because pay is computed per cycle and a cycle cannot be paid at two rates. "
                + "Give the first day of the month the change applies from.");
        }
        SalaryHistory.SalaryRate rate = new SalaryHistory.SalaryRate(
            employeeId, effectiveFrom,
            new BigDecimal(requiredString(body, "monthlyBasic")),
            new BigDecimal(requiredString(body, "riceSubsidy")),
            new BigDecimal(requiredString(body, "phoneAllowance")),
            new BigDecimal(requiredString(body, "clothingAllowance")),
            body.has("reason") ? body.get("reason").getAsString() : "",
            java.time.Instant.now().toString());
        salaryHistory.add(rate);
        sendJson(exchange, 201, "{\"rate\":" + salaryRateToJson(rate) + "}");

## Scope and security

- No production employee or payroll records.
- No service account, Admin SDK, or privileged credentials.
- Current user-owned sandbox rules are development-only, not an organizational role model.
- Payroll formulas, pay-period logic, and calculations remain blocked until specified by supplied course materials.

## Payroll

Payroll is enabled and effective-dated. Every response that carries money returns decimal strings;
the client never does arithmetic on them.

| Method | Path | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| GET | `/api/payroll/rules?year=2026` | Ruleset id, effective window, rates, MSC bounds, both Annex E tables |
| GET | `/api/payroll/timesheet?employeeId=&from=&to=` | Stored timecard summary: `daysWorked`, `totalHours`, per-day rows |
| POST | `/api/payroll/preview` | Compute one payslip; `saved:false` |
| POST | `/api/payroll/runs` | Compute and persist an immutable run snapshot; `201` |
| GET | `/api/payroll/runs` | Run history with totals (no payslip bodies) |
| GET | `/api/payroll/runs/{runId}` | One saved run including every payslip line |

A typed `30` for February, a ten-day range, or a range spanning two months is refused with `400` and a reason. ## Salary history Rates are dated rows, not a field on the employee record, so a raise cannot rewrite a payslip that has already been paid. | Method | Path | Purpose | |---|---|---| | GET | `/api/payroll/salary-history?employeeId=` | Dated rates. Payroll and HR see everyone; anybody else sees only their own | | POST | `/api/payroll/salary-history` | Record a rate. A mid-month date is refused with `400` and that explanation. - Two rates for the same person and date are refused (`400`). - Opening rates are seeded from the supplied employee file, effective 2025-01-01, one row per person. - A run for a **declared cycle** must reconcile with the dated rate: submitting an amount that disagrees with the rate in force is refused (`400`) and names both figures. A bare `/api/payroll/preview` that names no cycle stays a calculator and uses the figures it is given. ## Scope and security - No production employee or payroll records; the data is the supplied MotorPH files. - No service account, Admin SDK, or privileged credentials. - Firestore Rules are in `docs/firestore.rules`. - The role seed for the 34 employees is a **demonstration assignment** based on their real positions, flagged as such in `/api/me`; it is not a personnel policy.''' assert old in s s = s.replace(old, new, 1) p.write_text(s) print('api contract updated') PY grep -c "" docs/api-contract.md

# Role model and access matrix — gap analysis

**Date:** 2026-11-06 · **Input:** your five role definitions, the RBAC matrix in `message (2).txt`,
and the permission diagram (5 nesting scopes + 8 permission bubbles).

This is an **analysis plus a plan**, not an implementation. Two of the five roles cannot be built
correctly on today's data model, and saying so now is cheaper than building a demo of them that has to
be thrown away.

---

| Role | What you asked for |
|---|---|
| **Employee** | Clock in/out, view own attendance, own salary tracker, submit tickets (Overtime, Leave, Timesheet, Payroll dispute, Tech support), view team members, check team leave |
| **Supervisor** | Everything Employees do **plus** manage team schedules, approve OT/leave, handle timesheet edits, and raise promotion / merit / bonus / disciplinary / unpaid-leave requests that change earnings |
| **Payroll** | Gross-to-net (earnings + OT + bonuses + allowances), statutory and voluntary deductions, disburse, remit, generate payslips |
| **HR** | Everything Supervisors do plus onboard/offboard, employee records, HR tickets |
| **System Admin** | Configuration, roles, security policies, full database access; immediate access to and approval of government details |

# Build status — persistent-only target

> **Payroll status update (2026-11-05):** payroll now calculates against an effective-dated
> ruleset and reproduces the supplied MotorPH payslip to the centavo. See
> `docs/payroll-ruleset-and-golden-case.md`. The statements below about a removed *temporary
> preview* remain historically accurate; what replaced it is a durable, saved-run feature, not a
> browser-only estimate.

**This document supersedes earlier statements that a process-memory product mode or a temporary payroll preview is an acceptable deliverable.** The user's current requirement is “No locals, no temps.” No peer implementation or earlier policy candidate changes that requirement.

## Product behavior now enforced

- `AppServer.main` requires `FIREBASE_PROJECT_ID`. The only no-Firebase entry-point exception is `MOTORPH_TEST_MODE=true` while binding to a loopback host; the production run scripts do not set it. Direct constructor-based local services remain test fixtures used by the isolated test harness, not a supported deployment mode.
- `web/app.js` does not open the workspace if Firebase web configuration is missing. It shows a setup error instead. The unauthenticated local workspace is available only in the test build flag `VITE_E2E_TEST_MODE=true` used by the test runner.
- Removed the browser-only 2026 payroll preview that existed on 2026-11-04. On 2026-11-05 it was replaced by a server-side, effective-dated payroll service grounded in MotorPH's supplied payslip and timecard: `PayrollService`, `PayrollRuleset`, `TimesheetService`, saved `PayrollRun` snapshots in Firestore, and payslip rendering in the Payroll view. The removed artefact was a synthetic-input estimate; the replacement stores its inputs, ruleset version and assumptions with every run.
- The test-only synthetic fixture remains intentionally process-memory-backed so the UI/API contract can be exercised without using real staff data or writing test records to a live Firebase project. This is test infrastructure, not a deployable local-data feature.

## Verified after these changes

- **The roster is now MotorPH's own file (2026-11-06).** The four invented `DEMO-` employees that
  shipped in the fixture are gone. `tools/generate_fixtures.py` reads
  `uploads/Copy of MotorPH_Employee Data - Employee Details.csv` and writes all **34 rows**
  (10001–10034) with the supplied names, positions, basic pay and three allowances into
  `InMemoryEmployeeStore.java`. Department is derived from position (the CSV has no department
  column); status is "Active" for all 34 because the CSV's `Status` column is employment type.
  12 test classes, 13 web test files and the e2e flow were re-pointed from `DEMO-00x` to the real
  numbers. New records now receive the next free five-digit number (10035 onward) instead of a
  `DEMO-<hex>` ID; `docs/firestore.rules` requires `^[0-9]{5}$`.
- **Employee pay is now editable (2026-11-06).** The HR editor previously exposed no pay fields, so
  "where do I change a rate?" had no answer. Monthly basic plus rice/phone/clothing allowances are
  now inputs on **HR → Employee records → Edit**, are sent with create/update, and are what payroll
  reads. Omitted pay fields keep their stored values. There is still **no effective-dated salary
  history** — stated on the screen and in `docs/api-contract.md`.
- **SSS salary credit corrected (2026-11-06).** The engine rounded the credit **up** to the next
  ₱500; SSS publishes ₱500-wide **brackets** (5,250.00–5,749.99 → 5,500.00). Round-up overstates
  the credit in the lower half of every bracket (₱10,001 → ₱10,500 instead of ₱10,000; ₱25,249 →
  ₱25,500 instead of ₱25,000). Now banded to the bracket. **No MotorPH employee was affected** —
  all 34 salaries sit above their bracket midpoint — so the golden payslip is unchanged.
  `PayrollGoldenTest` 65 → 70. The claim in `docs/sweldongpinoy-crosscheck.md` §4 that ceil and
  bracket banding were "verified identical" was wrong and has been withdrawn.

# MotorPH — the short guide

You don't need the 1,500-line version to understand this app.
**Read this file. Skim section 5. Look things up in the big file only when you want.**

---

## 1. What this app is, in 5 lines

1. It's a payroll app for MotorPH: people, timecards, leave, and payslips.
2. You sign in with your own account. You only ever see your own data.
3. It calculates a payslip **exactly like MotorPH's own sample payslip** — same numbers to the centavo.
4. It saves each payroll run permanently. You can reprint it later.
5. The **34 people are the real rows from MotorPH's employee file**. Only the sample timecards,
   leave and ticket records are invented, and each is labelled where it appears.

---

## 2. The 3 ideas that explain everything else

**Idea 1 — The browser never does maths.**
Every number on screen came from the server. The browser only prints it.
So if a number is wrong, the bug is on the server. Always.

**Idea 2 — The server never says "yes" to the database.**
The server passes your login token to Firebase, and **Firebase's rules** decide what you can see.
Your `uid` comes from your token — you cannot ask for someone else's data even by editing the request.

**Idea 3 — Money is never a float.**
Decimals are stored as text (`"26750.00"`) and calculated exactly. Rounding happens in exactly one

[NODE 12889]
idea 2 corrected
**Idea 2 — The server decides, from who you are.**
Two layers, and they do different jobs.

*Firebase's rules* guarantee you can only reach your own user's documents — your `uid` comes from your
token, so you cannot ask for someone else's storage even by editing the request.

*The role matrix* (`Policy.java`) decides what your employee number may see **within** that storage:
a supervisor gets their direct reports, HR gets the roster, an employee gets themselves. The server
resolves your role from your employee number — the browser never sends a role, and it never sends a
permission. Directory replies are filtered server-side, so a response cannot contain a row you may not
read, and a refusal comes back as a real `403` with a reason.

package ph.motorph.web;

/**
 * Resolves who is calling, once per request.
 *
 * <p>Two identity inputs are used, in this order:
 *
 * <ol>
 *   <li><b>Production (Firebase mode).</b> The signed-in account's employee number comes from the
 *       {@code X-Firebase-EID} header, which the server only honours when a bearer token is also
 *       present — the token is the authentication, the header only says which employee that account
 *       is. A token whose account has no employee link is treated as an Employee with no records,
 *       never as an administrator.</li>
 *   <li><b>Isolated test fixture.</b> The same header, with no token, because that mode has no
 *       authentication by design and never runs in production (the entry point refuses to start
 *       without Firebase unless bound to loopback in test mode).</li>
 * </ol>
 *
 * <p>The role always comes from {@link RoleAssignment}, never from a header, so a client cannot
 * promote itself by editing the request.
 */
public final class RequestActor {

    private RequestActor() {
    }

    /**
     * @param headerEmployeeId value of {@code X-Firebase-EID}, or null
     * @param authenticated    whether a verified bearer token accompanied the request
     * @param roles            the role assignment in force
     */
    public static AccessControl.Actor resolve(String headerEmployeeId, boolean authenticated,
                                              RoleAssignment roles) {
        String employeeNumber = headerEmployeeId == null ? "" : headerEmployeeId.trim();
        // A first-time user really has no employee number yet: their Firebase account exists but HR
        // has not linked it to a person. Refusing them outright would make self-registration
        // impossible, so an unlinked actuary is admitted as a role-less applicant who may read
        // nothing but may submit an access request. Every matrix cell for that role is NONE.
        if (employeeNumber.isEmpty() && authenticated) {
            return new AccessControl.Actor("", Role.APPLICANT);
        }
        if (!employeeNumber.matches("[0-9]{5}")) {
            throw new AccessControl.Denied(
                "This account is not linked to a MotorPH employee number. Ask HR to link it.",
                403);
        }
        if (!authenticated) {
            throw new AccessControl.Denied("Sign in with your MotorPH account to continue.", 401);
        }
        return new AccessControl.Actor(employeeNumber, roles.roleOf(employeeNumber));

    private FirestoreRestClient firestoreClientFor(HttpExchange exchange) {
        String authorization = exchange.getRequestHeaders().getFirst("Authorization");
        String uid = exchange.getRequestHeaders().getFirst("X-Firebase-UID");
        if (authorization == null || !authorization.startsWith("Bearer ") || uid == null || uid.trim().isEmpty()) {
            throw new FirestoreException("Sign in with your Firebase account to continue.", 401);
        }
        String token = authorization.substring("Bearer ".length()).trim();
        if (token.length() > 8192 || uid.length() > 128 || uid.contains("/")) {
            throw new FirestoreException("Invalid Firebase session information.", 401);
        }
        return firestoreApiRoot == null
            ? new FirestoreRestClient(firebaseProjectId, uid, token)
            : new FirestoreRestClient(firebaseProjectId, uid, token, firestoreApiRoot);
    }

    private static LocalDate parseOptionalDate(String value) {
        return value == null || value.trim().isEmpty() ? null : LocalDate.parse(value.trim());
    }

    /** The employee record lookup used to resolve team membership. */

    /**
     * Checks one operation against one employee.
     *
     * @param targetEmployeeNumber the record being touched (for a list call, call this per row)
     * @throws Denied with 403 when the matrix forbids it
     */
    public void require(Actor actor, Policy.Entity entity, Policy.Operation operation, String targetEmployeeNumber) {
        if (actor == null) throw new Denied("Sign in with your MotorPH account to continue.", 401);
        Policy.Scope scope = Policy.scope(entity, actor.role());

        if (scope == Policy.Scope.NONE) {
            throw new Denied(actor.role().label() + " has no access to " + entity.label() + ".", 403);
        }
        if (scope == Policy.Scope.APPROVAL_REQUIRED) {
            throw new Denied(entity.label() + " changes are approved, not applied directly.", 403);
        }
        if (operation != Policy.Operation.READ && !Policy.allows(entity, actor.role(), operation)) {
            throw new Denied(actor.role().label() + " may not " + operation.name().toLowerCase()
                + " " + entity.label() + ".", 403);
        }

        boolean own = targetEmployeeNumber != null && targetEmployeeNumber.equals(actor.employeeNumber());
        switch (scope) {
            case READ_SELF:
                if (!own) throw new Denied("You may only see your own " + entity.label().toLowerCase() + ".", 403);
                return;

package ph.motorph.web;

import java.util.Collections;
import java.util.LinkedHashMap;
import java.util.Map;

/**
 * Who is which role.
 *
 * <p>In MotorPH's database this is the relation between an account and a role. Until the tenancy
 * work in {@code docs/role-model-and-access-matrix.md} is built, it is kept in one explicit map so
 * that no code path has to guess: an employee number that is not in this map is an
 * {@link Role#EMPLOYEE} and nothing more.
 *
 * <p>The seed below is a <b>demonstration assignment, not MotorPH policy</b>. It follows the
 * positions in their own employee file (Chief Financial Officer, HR Manager, Payroll Manager,
 * System Admin) so the matrix can be exercised end to end with real names and numbers.
 */
public final class RoleAssignment {

    private final Map<String, Role> roles;

    public RoleAssignment(Map<String, Role> roles) {
        this.roles = Collections.unmodifiableMap(new LinkedHashMap<>(roles));
    }

    /** The five roles mapped onto MotorPH's own positions, for demonstration. */
    public static RoleAssignment demoSeed() {
        Map<String, Role> seed = new LinkedHashMap<>();
        // System Admin — IT Operations and Systems (10005, Eduard Hernandez).
        seed.put("10005", Role.SYSTEM_ADMIN);
        // HR — HR Manager, HR Team Leader, HR Rank and File.
        seed.put("10006", Role.HR);
        seed.put("10007", Role.HR);
        seed.put("10008", Role.HR);
        seed.put("10009", Role.HR);
        // Payroll — Payroll Manager, Payroll Team Leader, Payroll Rank and File,
        // and the Accounting Head who owns the payroll register (10010).
        seed.put("10010", Role.PAYROLL);
        seed.put("10011", Role.PAYROLL);

private void handleMe(HttpExchange exchange) throws IOException {
        if (!"GET".equals(exchange.getRequestMethod())) {
            sendJson(exchange, 405, "{\"error\":\"Method not allowed\"}");
            return;
        }
        try {
            AccessControl.Actor actor = actorFor(exchange);
            EmployeeService service = servicesFor(exchange).employeeService;
            Optional<Employee> self = service.findEmployee(actor.employeeNumber());
            AccessControl control = accessControlFor(exchange);

            JsonObject o = new JsonObject();
            o.addProperty("employeeNumber", actor.employeeNumber());
            o.addProperty("role", actor.role().name());
            o.addProperty("roleLabel", actor.role().label());
            o.addProperty("name", self.map(Employee::getName).orElse(""));
            o.addProperty("position", self.map(Employee::getRole).orElse(""));
            o.addProperty("department", self.map(Employee::getDepartment).orElse(""));
            o.addProperty("supervisorId", self.map(Employee::getSupervisorId).orElse(null));
            o.addProperty("hasPayProfile", self.map(Employee::hasPayProfile).orElse(false));

            JsonArray reports = new JsonArray();
            for (Employee candidate : service.listEmployees()) {
                if (actor.employeeNumber().equals(candidate.getSupervisorId())) {
                    JsonObject row = new JsonObject();
                    row.addProperty("id", candidate.getId());
                    row.addProperty("name", candidate.getName());
                    reports.add(row);
                }
            }
            o.add("directReports", reports);
            o.add("permissions", permissionMatrixFor(actor));
            o.addProperty("roleSeedIsDemonstration", true);
            sendJson(exchange, 200, o.toString());
        } catch (AccessControl.Denied denied) {

  const headers = { Accept: 'application/json', ...extra };
  if (state.user) {
    const token = await state.user.getIdToken();
    headers.Authorization = `Bearer ${token}`;

        private void savePayrollRun(String path, String body) {
            String documentId = "";
            int query = path.indexOf('?');
            if (query >= 0) {
                for (String pair : path.substring(query + 1).split("&")) {
                    if (pair.startsWith("documentId=")) documentId = pair.substring("documentId=".length());
                }
            }
            String cleanPath = query >= 0 ? path.substring(0, query) : path;
            com.google.gson.JsonObject parsed = com.google.gson.JsonParser.parseString(body).getAsJsonObject();
            storedRunFields = parsed.getAsJsonObject("fields").toString();
            storedRunName = "projects/demo-project/databases/(default)/documents"
                + cleanPath.substring(cleanPath.indexOf("/users/")) + "/" + documentId;
        }

        private String storedPayrollRun() {
            if (storedRunName == null) return "{}";
            return "{\"name\":\"" + storedRunName + "\",\"fields\":" + storedRunFields + "}";
        }

            server = HttpServer.create(new java.net.InetSocketAddress("127.0.0.1", 0), 0);

line meant the employee number — and therefore the role — came from a header the caller controlled.

[NODE 13753]
Any non-empty Authorization header counted as "signed in". The token was never verified — not its signature, not its expiry, not which project minted it. And the employee number came from a header you control. So two crafted headers made anyone the System Admin. Everything I said about "the browser can't promote itself" was true of the browser and false of curl.

[NODE 13754]
Authorization

[NODE 13755]
curl

[NODE 13756]
That's why five accounts felt necessary: with no real identity layer, an account was just a label, and the only way to get distinct labels was more of them.

[NODE 13757]
Identity is now verified. FirebaseTokenVerifier calls Google's accounts:lookup — signature, expiry, project all checked, cached two minutes, and a verification outage fails closed with 503 rather than becoming a bypass. FIREBASE_API_KEY is now required at startup; without it the process refuses to boot, because an unverified token is no authentication at all.

[NODE 13758]
FirebaseTokenVerifier

[NODE 13759]
accounts:lookup

[NODE 13760]
FIREBASE_API_KEY

[NODE 13761]
An account is not a person, and a person is not a role. That was the modelling mistake. A person holds a set of seats; an account links to one or more people. MotorPH's own file already had multi-seat people — 10006 is an HR Manager who also supervises 10007, so she legitimately acts as HR for the roster and Supervisor for her team. Giving her exactly one role forced a choice the business doesn't make.

[NODE 13762]
So there's now a seat switcher in the top bar. One login, several seats.

The perspective: 1000px also sits on each .receipt__half independently, not on a shared parent, so the two halves aren't quite folding in the same 3D space.

### New Base
https://github.com/Sitramonicus/forreview/tree/main/motorph-ms2-main/motorph-ms2-main This is what claude did and we'll use it as base.

### Code Rules: 

I usually put same data type declarations in one declaration line (separated with commas), but if I try to group them up if I have many of the same data type declaration (i.e., word wrap length, more than 4 variables in one line, etc.)

If I have only a few variables and functions in the file, then I just use lowercase with m_memberCase (or Member Notation) (ab_name; a = package/folder group (e.g., a for the a_doc folder), b = prefix for the group of variables (e.g., p for philhealth), name = var name), especially if it's just two words, but if it's more than two then switch to camelCase (still with member notation).

If it's not a few variables, I mix m_memberCase (or Member Notation) with Hungarian Notation (ab_dtName (a = package/folder group (e.g., a for the a_doc folder), b = prefix for the group of variables (e.g., p for philhealth), dt = data type, Name = var name))

Naming convention for files, still pascal case but inconsistent abbreveation (stuff that are easy to under stand like Emp = Employee is alright, but Atten = attendance is not. You also cant use FS for Firestore, but you can use Hday for holiday. You can use Gov for Government and Sched for Schedule but not Pht for Photos nor WF/WoFo for workflow. You can say Svc for Service but not Cdr for Calendar. Mem and Req can be shortenen but Mut for mutable is no go. Payslip cant be PS. Details can be Deet. There are a lot more that I cant account for, but basically use that logical/illogical notion)

---

1. Session ID Fundamentals

• What it is: A Session ID is a random string (like a digital ID badge) that links a user's browser to their data on the server.
• Security Rule: It must be a completely random, opaque string (e.g., 32 random bytes). It should never contain meaningful data like timestamps or user IDs, as this exposes system logic to attackers.
• Storage:
	• Browser: Stored in a secure HttpOnly cookie.
	• Server: Stored in a database (SQL, Redis) or memory to validate the user.

2. Session Lifespans

There are two critical clocks ticking for every session:
1. Inactivity Timeout (Idle Limit):
	• Purpose: Logs out a user if they stop interacting with the page (e.g., walk away for lunch).
	• Standard Duration: 15–30 minutes for sensitive apps (payroll, banking); longer for social media.
	• Reset Mechanism: Every click or request resets this timer to zero.
2. Absolute Timeout (Hard Limit):
	• Purpose: Forces a re-login after a set period regardless of activity, ensuring long-running sessions don't become security risks.
	• Standard Duration: 8–12 hours (matches a workday).
	• Reset Mechanism: Does not reset. Once the time is up, the session dies.

3. The Architecture: How to Handle Expiration

We explored three ways to manage these timeouts, concluding that Option C is the industry standard for production apps.

Approach	How it works	Verdict
A. Timestamp inside ID	Embedding the expiration date inside the Session ID string (e.g., ID_12:00PM).	Don't do this. It leaks server info, complicates database cleanup (heavy string parsing), and reduces security.
B. Per-Tick Loop	Running a background script that checks every second: "Is it expired yet?"	Inefficient. Wastes CPU power and doesn't scale well for thousands of users.
C. Event-Driven (Lazy)	The server does nothing until a user makes a request. Then it checks timestamps.	Best Practice. Zero CPU waste. The database cleans itself only when needed.


4. Implementation Guide


The Database Schema

Store session metadata in columns, not the ID string.
sql
TABLE sessions (
    session_id  VARCHAR  PRIMARY KEY, -- The random token
    user_id     INT,                  -- Who owns it
    last_active TIMESTAMP,            -- Updates on every click
    expires_at  TIMESTAMP             -- The hard deadline (8 hrs from login)
);
Use code with caution.

The Logic Flow (The "Lazy" Check)

This logic runs on every incoming HTTP request:
1. Check 1 (Idle): Is (Current Time - last_active) > 15 mins?
	• Yes: Delete session → Redirect to Login.
	• No: Continue.
2. Check 2 (Hard Limit): Is Current Time > expires_at?
	• Yes: Delete session → Redirect to Login.
	• No: Update last_active to Current Time → Allow access.

The Frontend "Auto-Logout"

Since the server cannot see if a user walked away, use JavaScript to handle the UI:
• Script: Listen for mouse/keyboard events.
• Action: If no events occur for 15 minutes, redirect the user to the login page immediately.
• Security Note: This is just for UX. The real security is the server-side check above.

Cleanup (The "Garbage Collector")

To remove abandoned sessions (users who closed the tab without logging out):
• SQL: Run a daily job: DELETE FROM sessions WHERE last_active < NOW() - INTERVAL '15 MIN'.
• Redis: Use native TTL (Time-To-Live). Redis automatically deletes the key when the timer hits zero—no code required.

---

1. Session ID Fundamentals

• What it is: A Session ID is a random string (like a digital ID badge) that links a user's browser to their data on the server.
• Security Rule: It must be a completely random, opaque string (e.g., 32 random bytes). It should never contain meaningful data like timestamps or user IDs, as this exposes system logic to attackers.
• Storage:
	• Browser: Stored in a secure HttpOnly cookie.
	• Server: Stored in a database (SQL, Redis) or memory to validate the user.

2. Session Lifespans

There are two critical clocks ticking for every session:
1. Inactivity Timeout (Idle Limit):
	• Purpose: Logs out a user if they stop interacting with the page (e.g., walk away for lunch).
	• Standard Duration: 15–30 minutes for sensitive apps (payroll, banking); longer for social media.
	• Reset Mechanism: Every click or request resets this timer to zero.
2. Absolute Timeout (Hard Limit):
	• Purpose: Forces a re-login after a set period regardless of activity, ensuring long-running sessions don't become security risks.
	• Standard Duration: 8–12 hours (matches a workday).
	• Reset Mechanism: Does not reset. Once the time is up, the session dies.

3. The Architecture: How to Handle Expiration

We explored three ways to manage these timeouts, concluding that Option C is the industry standard for production apps.

Approach	How it works	Verdict
A. Timestamp inside ID	Embedding the expiration date inside the Session ID string (e.g., ID_12:00PM).	Don't do this. It leaks server info, complicates database cleanup (heavy string parsing), and reduces security.
B. Per-Tick Loop	Running a background script that checks every second: "Is it expired yet?"	Inefficient. Wastes CPU power and doesn't scale well for thousands of users.
C. Event-Driven (Lazy)	The server does nothing until a user makes a request. Then it checks timestamps.	Best Practice. Zero CPU waste. The database cleans itself only when needed.


4. Implementation Guide


The Database Schema

Store session metadata in columns, not the ID string.
sql
TABLE sessions (
    session_id  VARCHAR  PRIMARY KEY, -- The random token
    user_id     INT,                  -- Who owns it
    last_active TIMESTAMP,            -- Updates on every click
    expires_at  TIMESTAMP             -- The hard deadline (8 hrs from login)
);
Use code with caution.

The Logic Flow (The "Lazy" Check)

This logic runs on every incoming HTTP request:
1. Check 1 (Idle): Is (Current Time - last_active) > 15 mins?
	• Yes: Delete session → Redirect to Login.
	• No: Continue.
2. Check 2 (Hard Limit): Is Current Time > expires_at?
	• Yes: Delete session → Redirect to Login.
	• No: Update last_active to Current Time → Allow access.

The Frontend "Auto-Logout"

Since the server cannot see if a user walked away, use JavaScript to handle the UI:
• Script: Listen for mouse/keyboard events.
• Action: If no events occur for 15 minutes, redirect the user to the login page immediately.
• Security Note: This is just for UX. The real security is the server-side check above.

Cleanup (The "Garbage Collector")

To remove abandoned sessions (users who closed the tab without logging out):
• SQL: Run a daily job: DELETE FROM sessions WHERE last_active < NOW() - INTERVAL '15 MIN'.
• Redis: Use native TTL (Time-To-Live). Redis automatically deletes the key when the timer hits zero—no code required.

---

• What they see:
	• Complete organizational salary data, including executive and board compensation.
	• High-level workforce analytics (e.g., revenue per employee, total headcount spend by department).
• System Action: Viewing dashboard analytics and running long-term labor cost projections.

⚙️ Chief Operating Officer (COO)

The COO focuses on operational efficiency, productivity, and department-level staffing costs.
• Access Level: Read-Only (Operational/Departmental Visibility).
• What they see:
	• Overtime (OT) trends, holiday pay, and absenteeism costs across operations and plants.
	• Departmental labor budgets to see which teams are over-utilizing resources.
	• Contractor and vendor billing vs. regular employee payroll costs.
• System Action: Monitoring labor efficiency metrics and approving department-specific structural changes.

📣 Chief Marketing Officer (CMO)

The CMO operates like a standard Department Head in the system, with access strictly limited to their own team.
• Access Level: Restricted Department Head / Manager Access.
• What they see:
	• Only the compensation, bonuses, and timesheets of the Marketing Department employees.
	• They have zero visibility into the salaries of Finance, Operations, IT, or other C-level peers.
• System Action: Approving timesheets, leaves, and commission/bonus requests for marketing staff before it goes to HR and Payroll Staff.
---

If you notice in claude's version, there are branches. What I want you to do regarding that is average out the logical middle ground between the teams (teams with no extra teams under them (e.g., Mata and De Leon, but not Romualdez) using their addresses listed in the csv then set them to that branch. For those with employees under them that aren't directly handled by them and C-level employees, just put them in the "Main Branch."

Other stuff need populating: Payroll use [Copy of MotorPH_Employee Data - Employee Details.csv] to make a plausible payroll for each employee and attendance to back that up (taking into account stuff that has extra pay, etc.). Use [Copy of MotorPH Sample Timecard - MotorPH Payslip.csv] as well as a sort of basis.

In the video, a developer used Lean 4 (a functional programming language and theorem prover) to build a highly optimized web server for a "$12 server challenge" (0:19).
The core optimizations and performance details include:

[NODE 13892]
Database Optimizations

[NODE 13893]
• Direct B-Tree Access: Instead of using SQLite's standard query execution engine, the developer used Lean 4 to prove specific mathematical properties about the data layout (0:34). They verified that the posts were already sorted in the correct order (0:44). This allowed them to bypass the SQL engine entirely and read directly from SQLite's underlying B-tree API (0:49).
• Latency Reduction: This database shortcut slashed the time required to load the feed from 16.7 microseconds down to just 5.4 microseconds (roughly 3x faster) (1:00).

[NODE 13894]
System Optimizations

[NODE 13895]
• Optimized Code Generation: The formal proofs written in Lean 4 were used to safely generate highly optimized C code (0:34).
• I/O Optimization: The developer utilized io_uring for asynchronous system calls, a technique shared by top-performing submissions in the challenge (1:18).

[NODE 13896]
Final Performance Results

[NODE 13897]
When benchmarked on a small server with just 1 vCPU and 2 GB of RAM, the submission successfully handled (0:10):
• Over 280,000 concurrent users (1:18)
• 26,000 requests per second (1:23)
If you're interested in building highly performant APIs, let me know if you would like to explore:
How Lean 4 works as both a programming language and a mathematical theorem proverThe mechanics behind Linux's io_uring and why it speeds up backend I/OHow to safely optimize SQLite for high-concurrency workloads

# MotorPH MS2 — Implementation Brief

## 1. Objective

Continue the MotorPH employee and payroll application using Claude's implementation as the primary starting point:

**Primary base repository:** https://github.com/Sitramonicus/forreview/tree/main/motorph-ms2-main/motorph-ms2-main

The existing project in the current workspace contains changes and corrections that were not included in the instructions given to Claude. Compare both implementations first, then use Claude's version as the main base while retaining relevant improvements from the current workspace. Do not blindly replace the current project or discard later corrections.

The expected result is a functioning, populated MotorPH employee and payroll application, with the requested authentication, employee hierarchy, access controls, branch assignments, attendance, payroll, and UI changes implemented in the project itself. This is an implementation task, not merely an audit or a proposed plan.

Work through the requirements in this document without stopping after the comparison. Make reasonable, clearly documented assumptions where the supplied material does not settle a detail. Do not ask me to repeat information already present here or in the project files.

## 2. Required initial inspection

Before changing code:

1. Inspect the current workspace, its project structure, build configuration, application entry points, persistence layer, tests, and existing documentation.
2. Retrieve and inspect the primary base repository above. If it cannot be accessed, state the exact blocker and continue with the files available locally. Do not claim to have compared code that you could not access.
3. Locate and read `skills_compilation.md`. Search it for the skills relevant to this task, including Java/backend development, frontend development, application architecture, authentication and session security, database design, accessibility, CSS, testing, linting, and performance. Read and apply the applicable skill instructions before implementing their respective areas. Do not indiscriminately apply unrelated skills.
4. Compare the current implementation with Claude's implementation. Identify changes in behaviour, data structures, calculations, security, UI, dependencies, and documentation. Pay particular attention to later fixes and dated systems that were already changed in the current implementation.
5. Produce a concise comparison record with three classifications:
   - **Keep from Claude:** the preferred implementation or UI to retain.
   - **Keep from current project:** a later correction or useful feature missing from Claude's copy.
   - **Replace or reconcile:** outdated, conflicting, duplicated, or incomplete behaviour.
6. Use the following order of authority when sources disagree:
   1. Explicit requirements in this brief.
   2. Corrected behaviour already present in the current project, where it does not conflict with this brief.

   4. Existing project documentation and supplied CSV/timecard/payslip materials.
   5. External references and reasonable implementation assumptions.

Do not use the comparison as an excuse to stop. After recording the differences, implement the agreed result.

## 3. General implementation rules

- Preserve Claude's existing UI, colour scheme, branding, and MotorPH logo except where this brief explicitly requests a change.
- Preserve working behaviour unless it conflicts with an explicit requirement or is demonstrably defective.
- Prefer a small number of clear folders. Do not create a folder for every class or component.
- Keep the existing stack where it is suitable. Do not rewrite the entire application or introduce a new framework merely for preference.
- Replace Firebase Authentication with Employee ID and password authentication. Do not remove Firestore or another existing persistence service automatically if it can remain useful as the application's data store. Separate authentication from data persistence, then retain or replace the persistence layer based on what the inspected code supports.
- Do not leave non-functional buttons, placeholder pages, fake success messages, or controls that only look interactive.
- Do not hard-code secrets, password peppers, session tokens, or private configuration in source control.
- Keep calculations in testable backend/service modules rather than embedding business rules in UI event handlers.
- Avoid needless abstractions, excessive dependencies, and gratuitous rewrites.
- Use transactions or equivalent safeguards for changes that must remain consistent, particularly payroll runs, password changes, and approval actions.
- Make the application usable at desktop, tablet, and mobile widths. Maintain keyboard access, visible focus, sensible contrast, and reduced-motion support.
- Do not claim a test, benchmark, integration, or comparison succeeded unless you actually ran it and observed the result.

## 4. Naming and code-style preferences

Follow these conventions where they fit the language and existing code. Do not sacrifice valid syntax, standard tooling, or readability to force a notation into a place where it does not belong.

### Variable and member naming

- When several variables share the same data type and their names are short, group declarations on one line, separated by commas. Split them when the line becomes difficult to scan, wraps excessively, or contains more than roughly four variables.
- For files with only a few variables and functions, prefer lowercase member notation such as `ab_name`. The prefix letters identify the source package/folder group and variable group: for example, `a` can identify `a_doc`, and `p` can identify a PhilHealth-related group.
- For a small number of names containing more than two words, use camelCase after the member prefix.
- For larger files with many declarations, combine the member notation with Hungarian-style type prefixes, for example `ab_dtName`, where `dt` identifies the data type and `Name` is the variable name.
- Apply the notation consistently within a file. Do not rename every existing identifier solely to impose a new style if doing so would create needless churn.

### File naming

- Prefer PascalCase for file names.
- Abbreviations are selective rather than mechanically shortened. `Emp`, `Hday`, `Gov`, `Sched`, `Svc`, `Mem`, `Req`, and `Deet` are acceptable where clear. Avoid unclear abbreviations such as `Atten`, `Pht`, `WF`, `WoFo`, `Cdr`, and `PS` for payslip. Do not abbreviate Firestore as `FS`, or mutable as `Mut`.
- Prefer an understandable full word over an abbreviation when uncertain. Do not invent a new abbreviation merely to shorten a filename.
- Keep names consistent within a feature area.

## 5. Source and web folder organisation

Use the following organisation as the preferred structure. Add a folder only when its contents do not reasonably belong in an existing one. Keep the number of folders low.

### Application source

Under the main source directory, use:

- `a_doc` — project notes, technical documentation, decision records, and implementation references.
- `o_oop` — object-oriented models, entities, and core application objects.
- `t_tkt` — ticket, support-request, and related workflow code.
- `l_log` — logging and audit-related code.
- `c_calc` — payroll, statutory, and other calculation code.

Add another source folder only when a group has a clear responsibility that does not fit those five. Keep package declarations, imports, build files, and test paths valid after any relocation.

### Web application

Under `web/`, prefer:

- `b_basic` — primary GUI, pages, tabs, profiles, and their local components.
- `f_flares` — motion, animation, decorative effects, and dynamic visual elements.
- `sp_secpol` — security and policy-related UI, notices, and client-side security controls.

Organise tabs and profiles inside `b_basic` only where that separation improves navigation. Do not create deeply nested folders without a practical reason.

### Tests and quality tools

Create a conventional, easy-to-run test and quality structure. Retain the tests already used by Claude and the current project, then add the relevant checks below where compatible with the stack:

- Unit tests for Java services, models, authentication, permissions, calculations, and data transformations.
- Integration tests for persistence, API routes, sessions, payroll processing, and role restrictions.
- Frontend tests for components, forms, navigation, and state changes.
- End-to-end browser tests for login, logout, password change, role access, employee workflows, attendance, payroll, and payslips.
- JavaScript linting with ESLint, plus formatting checks where suitable.
- Java static analysis and style checks, including Checkstyle, SpotBugs, and PMD where compatible with the project's Java version and build system.
- CSS/HTML checks, accessibility checks, and responsive-layout checks.
- Lighthouse checks for accessibility, performance, best practices, and SEO where applicable to the application.
- Dependency and security auditing.

Do not add tools just to inflate the tool list. Configure the tools that are actually compatible, make them runnable through the project's normal scripts, and document any tool that could not be configured. Separate mandatory tests from optional audits so a network-dependent Lighthouse run does not make the ordinary unit-test command unusable.

## 6. Employee records and account provisioning

Use **`Copy of MotorPH_Employee Data - Employee Details.csv`** as the canonical employee source for all employee accounts and employee details.

- Import every employee represented in the CSV. Do not silently omit employees because their role or supervisor is inconvenient to map.
- Use the Employee ID as the login identifier. Do not require a Firebase account, email address, or external identity provider to sign in.
- Preserve employee details accurately. Normalise formatting only where needed for reliable storage and display; do not alter source facts without documenting the transformation.
- Handle duplicate, blank, or malformed Employee IDs explicitly. Do not create ambiguous accounts.
- Keep employee identity, reporting relationships, branch, role, and payroll data in fields that can be validated independently.
- Do not expose residential addresses, personal contact details, or other unnecessary personal information in general employee views.
- Apply access checks on the server/API and data-query layer. Hiding a button or tab is not an access-control mechanism.

### Initial passwords

Set the initial password for each imported employee account to the exact case-sensitive value:

`MotorPH-demo-2026`

This is an initial provisioning credential for testing the password-change flow. It must never be stored as plaintext in the database, logs, client code, or committed configuration.

Implement password storage with:

- A modern password-hashing algorithm, preferably Argon2id with an appropriate work factor for the deployment environment.
- A cryptographically random, unique salt for every account. Two employees who start with the same password must have different stored password hashes.
- A server-side pepper supplied through a protected environment variable or secret manager. Do not derive it from an Employee ID, email, name, birthday, location, timestamp, or other predictable/user-specific value. Never store the pepper beside the password hashes.
- A documented pepper-missing/start-up failure policy. Do not silently fall back to plaintext or a hard-coded pepper.
- Constant-time hash comparison through the selected password library.
- Rate limiting and sensible failed-login handling. Error messages must not reveal whether an Employee ID exists.

Set a `must_change_password` (or equivalent) flag for initially provisioned accounts and require the employee to choose a new password after the first successful login. Implement and test password changes, current-password verification, password policy validation, hash replacement, and session revocation/rotation. Do not display the shared initial password anywhere in the normal application interface.

## 7. Authentication and session management

Implement first-party Employee ID/password authentication and a server-validated session system. The following is the required behaviour; use a more efficient implementation where appropriate without weakening these guarantees.

### Session token

- Generate at least 32 cryptographically random bytes for each session token.
- Encode the token as an opaque URL-safe random string. It must not contain an Employee ID, timestamp, expiry, location, or other meaningful data.
- Send it to the browser in a cookie configured with `HttpOnly`, `SameSite=Lax` or stricter where the application permits, and `Secure` in HTTPS deployments. Set a narrow, appropriate `Path` and avoid broad domain scope.
- Store only a one-way hash of the session token on the server where practical, together with the employee/account reference and session metadata. Never store or log the raw token.
- Use the project's existing database/persistence service if it can safely store and validate sessions. If a separate sessions table/collection is appropriate, use fields equivalent to `session_id_hash`, `user_id`, `created_at`, `last_active`, and `expires_at`.

### Expiry rules

- Idle timeout: 15 minutes without authenticated activity.
- Absolute timeout: 8 hours from session creation, regardless of activity.
- Check both limits on every protected server request. Expired sessions must be rejected and invalidated.
- Refresh `last_active` from authenticated activity. Avoid a background loop that checks every second; use request-driven/lazy validation. Throttle writes if necessary, provided the 15-minute idle limit remains accurate enough for the application.

## 8. Reporting hierarchy, teams, and permissions

Use the immediate-supervisor information in the employee CSV to establish reporting relationships.

- Each employee belongs to the team led by their listed immediate supervisor, subject to the actual hierarchy represented in the data.
- A supervisor's roster includes their direct reports and all descendants in the reporting tree. For example, if Mata's team and De Leon's team report to Romualdez, Romualdez's roster must include both teams and their employees, including any nested reports.
- Do not treat every employee with a managerial-sounding job title as a supervisor unless the CSV or an explicit role mapping supports it.
- Detect missing supervisors, self-reporting, circular reporting chains, duplicate relationships, and employees who cannot be placed in the hierarchy. Do not silently invent reporting lines. Record exceptions and use a safe restricted default until resolved.
- A supervisor may see only their own team and descendant teams. They must not gain access to unrelated teams merely because they share a branch or department.
- Where a superior has subordinate supervisors, the superior's roster view must include those supervisors' teams recursively, not just immediate reports.

### Role and access model

Implement role-based permissions together with employee/team scope. A role determines the type of action available; the reporting tree determines which employee records the user may access. Treat this as a starting mapping and reconcile titles against the actual CSV and existing application roles.

| Role | Intended access |
|---|---|
| CEO | Read-only, company-wide oversight. May view workforce and high-level payroll cost information, including organisation-wide compensation visibility as required by the brief. No payroll editing or processing by default. |
| CFO | Broad financial visibility: payroll costs, statutory liabilities/remittances, compensation, and financial reports. Approval permissions may be enabled only where the application has an explicit approval workflow. Viewing payroll does not automatically grant authority to release funds or alter payroll. |
| COO | Operational visibility: department/team staffing, overtime, holiday work, attendance patterns, and operational labour-cost reports. Do not grant unrestricted access to all individual salary records unless the source data or an explicit permission requires it. |
| CMO | Treat as a supervisor-level account, limited to the CMO's own reporting chain. The CSV indicates a small team of three; verify the actual reporting rows and do not grant general C-level financial access. |
| Team supervisor | View and perform only the permitted actions for direct reports and descendant teams, such as leave or attendance approvals where those workflows exist. |
| HR staff | Employee administration and HR workflows within the permissions assigned to the HR role. Sensitive compensation access must be separately permissioned. |
| Payroll staff | Payroll preparation, calculation, review, and payslip operations as explicitly permitted. Separate preparation from final approval where feasible. |
| Employee | View their own profile, attendance, leave/requests, pay information, and payslips; submit permitted requests; change their password. |
| System administrator | Technical account and configuration administration. Administrative access must be explicit and audited; do not assume that a technical administrator automatically needs unrestricted salary visibility. |

Use least privilege. Keep approval, processing, viewing, and configuration permissions distinct. Record sensitive actions in an audit log with actor, action, target, time, and relevant outcome, while excluding passwords, raw session tokens, and unnecessary personal data.

## 9. Branch assignment

Use the branch list and branch names already present in Claude's implementation as the set of available branches. Do not invent extra branches unless the existing data makes that unavoidable and the reason is recorded.

Apply these rules:

1. For leaf teams — teams whose supervisor has no subordinate supervisors/teams beneath them, such as the Mata and De Leon teams in the example — estimate the team's geographic centre using the employee addresses in the CSV.
2. Use the available coordinates or a permitted geocoding method to derive a geographic centroid for the employees in each leaf team. Assign that team to the nearest existing branch using the branch's known location.
3. If an address cannot be geocoded reliably, use the most precise shared locality supported by the CSV. Do not fabricate coordinates or claim a precise midpoint where the source only supports a municipality/city-level estimate.
4. Do not upload the employee CSV or full residential addresses to an external geocoding service without explicit authorisation. Prefer existing coordinates, an offline/local source, or a locality-level approximation. Use addresses only for this assignment calculation, and do not expose them in the application UI or reports.
5. Supervisors who have subordinate supervisors/teams beneath them, and all C-level employees, must be assigned to **Main Branch**.
6. Employees in a leaf team inherit that leaf team's assigned branch unless the CSV contains a clear, documented exception.
7. Preserve the reporting hierarchy independently of branch assignment. Branch membership must not be used as a substitute for supervisor-based access control.

Document the resulting team-to-branch assignments and the method used. Where source addresses are insufficient, mark the assignment as approximate in engineering documentation rather than pretending it is exact.

## 10. Attendance and payroll population

Use both of the following supplied files:

- `Copy of MotorPH_Employee Data - Employee Details.csv` — employee identity, employment details, salary/rate information, and other employee-specific inputs.
- `Copy of MotorPH Sample Timecard - MotorPH Payslip.csv` — timecard, attendance, and payslip examples to guide the shape and treatment of payroll inputs and outputs.

Populate attendance and payroll records for every employee represented in the employee CSV.

### Attendance

- Use the sample timecard as the pattern for attendance fields and the handling of ordinary days, lateness, undertime, overtime, rest days, special days, regular holidays, night differential, and other supported cases.
- Respect each employee's applicable schedule, employment status, and payroll classification. Do not give every employee identical attendance.
- Create coherent attendance records across enough completed payroll periods to make employee histories, reports, and charts useful. Prefer at least the latest 12 completed monthly periods where the project supports monthly payroll. Do not invent a completed payroll for an unfinished period.
- Make attendance and payroll agree. Overtime, absences, lateness, leaves, holiday work, and other paid/unpaid time must reconcile with the corresponding payroll calculations.
- Avoid impossible or contradictory records, such as overlapping shifts, duplicate clock events, overtime outside a plausible shift, or paid leave that is also deducted as an absence.
- Where the employee CSV or sample timecard does not establish a value, choose a plausible assumption, document it in the data-generation notes, and keep it consistent across all affected records.

### Payroll

- Generate a plausible payroll history for every employee using the employee CSV and timecard/payslip material.
- Retain employee-specific salary rates, employment categories, allowances, and other applicable inputs where those are actually present in the sources.
- Calculate the gross pay, earnings, deductions, statutory contributions, withholding tax, and net pay through the application's calculation services. Do not randomly assign final payroll totals.
- Ensure every payslip item reconciles to its source attendance and payroll inputs. Totals must add correctly and round consistently to centavos.
- Implement or retain separate, testable calculations for ordinary pay, overtime, rest-day work, special non-working holidays, regular holidays, night differential, leave treatment, statutory deductions, and tax, to the extent supported by the source data and applicable rules.
- Verify Philippine statutory rates, thresholds, and payroll rules against current authoritative sources applicable to the payroll period. Keep effective dates and source references in the calculation documentation. Do not silently apply a 2026 rate to a different period if the rate changed.
- Do not present a provisional assumption as a statutory fact. Where a rule or employee classification is unavailable, document the assumption and make the result traceable.
- Support payroll preparation, review, approval (if applicable), processing, and payslip gene

## 13. Performance ideas from the Lean 4 server example

Use the supplied YouTube Short as inspiration, not as a requirement to reproduce its implementation:

https://www.youtube.com/shorts/Cr69N5pG258

The supplied description says the developer used Lean 4 proofs to justify direct access to SQLite's B-tree layout, reported a feed-load reduction from 16.7 μs to 5.4 μs, generated optimised C, and used `io_uring`. It also reports results of more than 280,000 concurrent users and 26,000 requests per second on a small server.

Evaluate which ideas make sense for this application's actual Java/backend, database, hosting, and workload. In particular:

- Measure current response times, query patterns, database access, and bottlenecks before optimising.
- Apply suitable indexes, query improvements, pagination, caching, reduced payloads, and efficient I/O where measurements justify them.
- Preserve transaction correctness, payroll accuracy, and access-control checks while optimising.
- Do not bypass a database engine's normal query layer or depend on undocumented storage internals unless the data layout and invariants can be proven and the maintenance cost is justified.
- Do not introduce Lean 4, generated C, SQLite B-tree shortcuts, or `io_uring` merely because the video used them. Adopt those only if they fit the actual stack and provide a measured benefit.
- Do not repeat the video's benchmark figures as if this application achieved them. Benchmark this application on the actual target environment and report the test conditions and results.

## 14. Security, privacy, and reliability requirements

In addition to authentication and role-based access above:

- Validate input on the server, including Employee IDs, date ranges, payroll values, and workflow transitions.
- Use parameterised queries or the equivalent safe data-access mechanism.
- Protect against injection, cross-site scripting, CSRF, insecure direct-object references, broken access control, and session fixation.
- Apply least-privilege access to employee records, attendance, compensation, reports, and payslips.
- Never expose one employee's payslip or personal data to another employee through guessed IDs or modified request parameters.
- Use secure password-reset/change flows and audit security-sensitive events.
- Avoid logging sensitive payroll fields, passwords, raw session tokens, or full residential addresses.
- Keep secrets in environment variables or an appropriate secret store, with example placeholders only in sample configuration.
- Use safe error handling. Do not expose stack traces or internal credentials to ordinary users.
- Use database constraints and validation to prevent duplicate payroll records and invalid employee relationships.
- Ensure payroll recalculation and processing are repeatable and do not create duplicate deductions or duplicate payment records.

Complete the work in this order, adjusting only where the repository's dependencies require it:

**Employee data and hierarchy**
