    /**
     * One thread drains deferred saves. It takes the snapshot under stateLock, so it never blocks
     * a request for longer than the copy itself, and stands aside when a foreground save is running.
     */
    private void startBackgroundWriter() {
        if (!deferSaves || dataFile == null) return;
        Thread writer = new Thread(() -> {
            long maxDelayMs = 150L;
            while (!Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()) {
                JsonObject snapshot = null;
                synchronized (stateLock) {
                    if (!stateDirty) {
                        saveInFlight = false;
                    } else if (!saveInFlight) {
                        saveInFlight = true;
                        stateDirty = false;
                        try {
                            snapshot = exportState();
                        } catch (RuntimeException ex) {
                            System.err.println("Could not snapshot state for saving: " + ex);
                        }
                    }
                }
                if (snapshot == null) {
                    synchronized (saveSignal) {
                        try {
                            saveSignal.wait(maxDelayMs);
                        } catch (InterruptedException stopping) {
                            Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
                        }
                    }
                    continue;
                }
                try {
                    dataFile.save(snapshot);
                } catch (IOException | RuntimeException ex) {
                    System.err.println("Could not save data to " + dataFile.describe() + ": " + ex);
                    synchronized (stateLock) {
                        stateDirty = true;
                    }
                }
            }
        }, "motorph-state-writer");
        writer.setDaemon(true);
        writer.start();
    }

    public void stop() {
        HttpServer stopping;
        synchronized (stateLock) {
            
        }
        return null;
    }

package ph.motorph.o_oop;

import com.google.gson.Gson;
import com.google.gson.GsonBuilder;
import com.google.gson.JsonElement;
import com.google.gson.JsonObject;
import com.google.gson.JsonParser;
import java.io.IOException;

/**
 * The same state document the file backend writes, stored in Firestore instead.
 *
 * Firestore caps a document at 1 MiB and the attendance store alone is ~940 KB, so the
 * stores are split across documents rather than kept in one blob:
 *
 *   objects/{storeName}        one document per store, for the small ones
 *   chunks/{store}_0000        a slice of an oversized store, joined back on load
 *
 * Every value is stored as a JSON string inside a single field. That keeps Firestore's
 * typed-value encoding out of the picture entirely -- what comes back is byte-identical
 * to what went in, so the pinned @SerializedName keys keep working untouched.
 */
public final class FirestoreStateStore implements StateStore {

    private static final int FORMAT_VERSION = 1;
    // Cutting on characters, not bytes: the payload is ASCII JSON, and a slice that splits a
    // multi-byte character would corrupt the reassembly. 700k chars stays under the 1 MiB cap.
    private static final int CHUNK_CHARS = 700_000;
    private static final String ROOT = "motorphState";
    // Firestore document paths must alternate collection/document, so a chunk cannot live at
    // motorphState/chunks/{id} (three segments after documents, which it rejects with
    // "lacks / at index N"). Chunks therefore live in their own top-level collection.
    private static final String CHUNKS = "motorphStateChunks";

    private final FirestoreRestClient fs_client;
    private final Gson fs_gson = new GsonBuilder()
        .registerTypeAdapter(LocalDate.class, text(LocalDate::parse))
        .registerTypeAdapter(LocalTime.class, text(LocalTime::parse))
        .registerTypeAdapter(LocalDateTime.class, text(LocalDateTime::parse))
        .registerTypeAdapter(YearMonth.class, text(YearMonth::parse))
        .disableHtmlEscaping()
        .create();

    public FirestoreStateStore(FirestoreRestClient fs_client) {
        this.fs_client = fs_client;
    }

    private interface Parser<T> { T apply(String value); }

    private static <T> com.google.gson.TypeAdapter<T> text(Parser<T> parse) {
        return new com.google.gson.TypeAdapter<T>() {
            @Override public void write(com.google.gson.stream.JsonWriter out, T value) throws IOException {
                if (value == null) { out.nullValue(); return; }
                out.value(value.toString());
            }
            @Override public T read(com.google.gson.stream.JsonReader in) throws IOException {
                if (in.peek() == com.google.gson.stream.JsonToken.NULL) { in.nextNull(); return null; }
                return parse.apply(in.nextString());
            }
        }.nullSafe();
    }

    @Override public Gson gson() { return fs_gson; }

    @Override public String backend() { return "firestore"; }

    @Override public String describe() { return "Firestore (" + ROOT + " collection)"; }

    @Override public Optional<JsonObject> load() throws IOException {
        JsonObject meta = readObject("_meta");
        if (meta == null) return Optional.empty();
        int format = meta.has("format") ? meta.get("format").getAsInt() : FORMAT_VERSION;
        if (format != FORMAT_VERSION) throw new IOException("Unknown Firestore state format: " + format);

        JsonObject stores = new JsonObject();
        JsonObject index = readObject("_index");
        if (index == null) return Optional.of(stores);

        for (String storeName : index.keySet()) {
            int chunks = index.get(storeName).getAsInt();
            StringBuilder joined = new StringBuilder();
            for (int part = 0; part < chunks; part++) {
                JsonObject chunk = readObject("chunks/" + storeName + "_" + String.format("%04d", part));
                if (chunk == null || !chunk.has("json")) {
                    throw new IOException("Firestore state is missing chunk " + part + " of " + storeName);
                }
                joined.append(chunk.get("json").getAsString());
            }
            stores.add(storeName, JsonParser.parseString(joined.toString()));
        }
        return Optional.of(stores);
    }

function freePort() {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    const probe = net.createServer();
    probe.once('error', reject);
    probe.listen(0, '127.0.0.1', () => {
      const { port } = probe.address();
      probe.close(() => resolve(port));
    });
  });
}

async function startServer(port) {
  child = spawn('java', [
    '-Xmx256m', '-XX:TieredStopAtLevel=1',
    '--add-modules', 'jdk.httpserver',
    '-cp', [gsonJar, bouncyJar, classes].join(path.delimiter),
    'ph.motorph.svc.AppServer'
  ], {
    cwd: projectRoot,
    env: {
      ...process.env,
      PORT: String(port),
      HOST: '127.0.0.1',
      WEB_ROOT: path.join(projectRoot, 'web'),
      MOTORPH_PEPPER: 'e2e-pepper-at-least-32-characters-long',
      LOCAL_DATA_FILE: path.join(scratch, 'state.json'),
      MOTORPH_SEED_FILE: path.join(scratch, 'state.json'),
      FIREBASE_PROJECT_ID: ''
    },
    stdio: ['ignore', 'pipe', 'pipe']
  });
  child.stderr.on('data', () => {});
  // A fresh data file is seeded and saved in full before the port opens, and provisioning the
  // 34 demo accounts costs one Argon2id hash each (about 9-10 s on two cores). Allow a generous
  // window so a loaded machine does not turn a slow start into a test failure.
  for (let i = 0; i < 450; i++) {
    try {
      const response = await fetch(`http://127.0.0.1:${port}/api/health`);
      if (response.ok) return;
      if (i % 25 === 0) console.log(`  waiting for the server (${response.status})...`);
    } catch {
      if (i % 25 === 0) console.log('  waiting for the server...');
    }
    await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 200));
  }
  throw new Error('server did not start');
}

async function stopServer() {
  if (!child) return;
  const done = new Promise(resolve => child.once('exit', resolve));
  child.kill('SIGTERM');
  await Promise.race([done, new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 5000))]);
  if (child.exitCode === null) child.kill('SIGKILL');
  child = null;
}

/** Sign in through the UI and return the page, already on the workspace. */
async function signIn(page, employeeId, { expectWrongCodeFirst = false } = {}) {
  await page.goto(`http://127.0.0.1:${page.__port}/signin`, { waitUntil: 'domcontentloaded' });
  await page.waitForTimeout(800);
  await page.fill('#auth-employee', employeeId);
  await page.fill('#auth-password', password);
  await page.click('#sign-in-button');
  await page.waitForFunction(() => !document.getElementById('code-form').hidden, null, { timeout: timeoutMs });

  if (expectWrongCodeFirst) {
    await page.fill('#code-input', '000000');
    await page.click('#code-verify-button');
    await page.waitForFunction(
      () => !document.getElementById('auth-error').hidden,
      null,
      { timeout: timeoutMs }
    ).catch(() => {});
    const error = (await page.textContent('#auth-error')) || '';
    assert.match(error, /wrong code|tries/i, `a wrong 2FA code is refused (got: ${error})`);
    assert.equal(await page.isVisible('.nav-item'), false, 'a wrong code still shows no workspace');
  }

  const preview = await page.textContent('#code-preview');
  const code = (preview.match(/\d{6}/) || [])[0];
  assert.ok(code, 'the demo deployment shows the code under the input');
  await page.fill('#code-input', code);
  await page.click('#code-verify-button');
  await page.waitForSelector('.nav-item:visible', { timeout: timeoutMs })
    .catch(() => {});
  await page.waitForTimeout(1800);
  assert.ok(await page.isVisible('.nav-item'), `employee ${employeeId} reaches the workspace`);
}

#!/usr/bin/env sh
set -eu
cd "$(dirname "$0")"
case "$(uname -s)" in MINGW*|MSYS*|CYGWIN*) S=";" ;; *) S=":" ;; esac

sh tools/build.sh --with-tests
CP="lib/gson-2.13.2.jar${S}lib/bcprov-jdk18on-1.78.1.jar${S}target/classes${S}target/test-classes"

fail=0
pass=0
for f in $(find src/test/java -name '*Test.java' | sort); do
  cls=$(printf '%s' "$f" | sed 's|src/test/java/||; s|/|.|g; s|\.java$||')
  if java --add-modules jdk.httpserver -cp "$CP" "$cls" 2>&1 | tee /tmp/motorph-test-out.txt | grep -q "^FAIL"; then
    echo "FAILED: $cls"
    cat /tmp/motorph-test-out.txt
    fail=$((fail + 1))
  else
    tail -n 1 /tmp/motorph-test-out.txt | sed "s|^|$cls: |"
    pass=$((pass + 1))
  fi
done

if command -v node >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  echo "---- web unit tests ----"
  if node --test test/web/*.test.js 2>&1 | tee /tmp/motorph-web-out.txt | tail -n 8 | grep -q "^# fail 0"; then
    grep -E "^# (tests|pass|fail)" /tmp/motorph-web-out.txt | sed 's/^# /web: /'
    pass=$((pass + 1))
  else
    echo "web unit tests FAILED"
    grep -E "^not ok" /tmp/motorph-web-out.txt | head -10
    fail=$((fail + 1))
  fi
fi

# The browser suite needs playwright-core and a Chromium binary; skip it cleanly when absent
# instead of failing a machine that has neither.
if [ "${MOTORPH_SKIP_E2E:-0}" = "1" ]; then
  echo "e2e: skipped (MOTORPH_SKIP_E2E=1)"
elif [ -d node_modules/playwright-core ] && [ -x "${CHROMIUM_PATH:-/home/user/.cache/ms-playwright/chromium-1248/chrome-linux64/chrome}" ]; then
  echo "---- browser e2e ----"
  if node test/e2e/local-workflows.e2e.js > /tmp/motorph-e2e-out.txt 2>&1; then
    tail -n 1 /tmp/motorph-e2e-out.txt
    pass=$((pass + 1))
  else
    echo "browser e2e FAILED"
    grep -E "^FAIL|^PASS|^[0-9]/5" /tmp/motorph-e2e-out.txt | tail -8
    fail=$((fail + 1))
  fi
else
  echo "e2e: skipped (playwright-core or Chromium not present)"
fi

echo "----"
echo "suites passed: $pass   failed: $fail"
[ "$fail" -eq 0 ]

package ph.motorph.o_oop;

import com.google.gson.Gson;
import com.google.gson.JsonObject;
import java.io.IOException;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Optional;

/**
 * Where the whole application state lives between requests.
 *
 * Two backends implement it: {@code LocalStateFile} writes one JSON file on disk,
 * {@code FirestoreStateStore} writes the same shape to Firestore. AppServer only ever
 * talks to this interface, so switching is an env-var decision, not a code change.
 */
public interface StateStore {

    Optional<JsonObject> load() throws IOException;

    void save(JsonObject stores) throws IOException;

    Gson gson();

    String describe();

    /** Short key the web UI shows: memory, file or firestore. */
    default String backend() { return "file"; }

    default List<String> listBackups() throws IOException { return new java.util.ArrayList<>(); }

    default JsonObject loadBackup(String name) throws IOException {
        throw new IOException("This state store keeps no backups.");
    }

    default String backupNow(String reason) throws IOException {
        throw new IOException("This state store keeps no backups.");
    }

    default String writeArchive(String prefix, com.google.gson.JsonElement content) throws IOException {
        throw new IOException("This state store keeps no archives.");
    }

    default String backupFolder() { return ""; }

    /** Where the state lives, for the startup banner. */
    default String location() { return describe(); }

    /**
     * A file that could not be parsed is moved aside so the server can start empty. A remote
     * store has nothing to move, so it reports where the unreadable copy was left instead.
     */
    /** Moves unreadable state out of the way. Remote stores have nothing to move: return null. */
    default String setAside() throws IOException {
        return null;
    }
}

package ph.motorph.l_log;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Collections;
import java.util.List;

public final class AuditLog {
    static final int lg_iKeep = 1000;
    static final int lg_iBatch = 500;

    public static final class Entry {
        public final String lg_sAt, lg_sActor, lg_sMethod, lg_sPath, lg_sTarget;
        public final int lg_iStatus;

        Entry(String lg_sAt, String lg_sActor, String lg_sMethod, String lg_sPath, String lg_sTarget, int lg_iStatus) {
            this.lg_sAt = lg_sAt;
            this.lg_sActor = lg_sActor;
            this.lg_sMethod = lg_sMethod;
            this.lg_sPath = lg_sPath;
            this.lg_sTarget = lg_sTarget;
            this.lg_iStatus = lg_iStatus;
        }
    }

    public interface Archiver {
        String archive(List<Entry> oldest);
    }

    private final List<Entry> lg_lEntries = new ArrayList<>();
    private final List<String> lg_lArchives = new ArrayList<>();

    public synchronized void record(String at, String actor, String method, String path, String target, int status, Archiver archiver) {
        lg_lEntries.add(new Entry(at, actor, method, path, target == null ? "" : target, status));
        if (lg_lEntries.size() > lg_iKeep) {
            List<Entry> lg_lOldest = new ArrayList<>(lg_lEntries.subList(0, lg_iBatch));
            String lg_sName = archiver == null ? null : archiver.archive(lg_lOldest);
            lg_lEntries.subList(0, lg_iBatch).clear();
            if (lg_sName != null) lg_lArchives.add(lg_sName);
        }
    }

    public synchronized List<Entry> search(String actor, String pathContains, boolean failuresOnly, int limit) {
        List<Entry> lg_lFound = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int lg_iIdx = lg_lEntries.size() - 1; lg_iIdx >= 0 && lg_lFound.size() < limit; lg_iIdx--) {
            Entry lg_eRow = lg_lEntries.get(lg_iIdx);
            if (!actor.isEmpty() && !lg_eRow.lg_sActor.equals(actor) && !lg_eRow.lg_sTarget.equals(actor)) continue;
            if (!pathContains.isEmpty() && !lg_eRow.lg_sPath.contains(pathContains)) continue;
            if (failuresOnly && lg_eRow.lg_iStatus < 400) continue;
            lg_lFound.add(lg_eRow);
        }
        return lg_lFound;
    }

    public synchronized int size() { return lg_lEntries.size(); }

    public synchronized List<String> archives() { return Collections.unmodifiableList(new ArrayList<>(lg_lArchives)); }
}
package ph.motorph.o_oop;

import com.google.gson.Gson;
import com.google.gson.GsonBuilder;
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;
import java.nio.file.Files;
import java.nio.file.Path;
import java.time.LocalDate;
import java.time.LocalTime;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.LinkedHashMap;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;

public final class StateFileRoundTripTest {
    private static int checks;

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        Path sample = Path.of("data/local-demo.json");
        if (!Files.exists(sample)) {
            System.out.println("SKIP no local-demo.json to read");
            return;
        }

        Gson gson = new GsonBuilder()
            .registerTypeAdapter(LocalDate.class, (com.google.gson.JsonSerializer<LocalDate>) (v, t, c) -> new com.google.gson.JsonPrimitive(v.toString()))
            .registerTypeAdapter(LocalDate.class, (com.google.gson.JsonDeserializer<LocalDate>) (v, t, c) -> LocalDate.parse(v.getAsString()))
            .registerTypeAdapter(LocalTime.class, (com.google.gson.JsonSerializer<LocalTime>) (v, t, c) -> new com.google.gson.JsonPrimitive(v.toString()))
            .registerTypeAdapter(LocalTime.class, (com.google.gson.JsonDeserializer<LocalTime>) (v, t, c) -> LocalTime.parse(v.getAsString()))
            .create();

        String raw = new String(Files.readAllBytes(sample), StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
        State state = gson.fromJson(raw, State.class);

        List<AttendanceRecord> rows = state.stores.attendance.records;
        check(rows.size() > 0, "attendance rows survive a load (" + rows.size() + ")");
        if (rows.size() > 0) {
            AttendanceRecord first = rows.get(0);
            check(first.getAttendanceId() > 0, "attendanceId is not blanked: " + first.getAttendanceId());
            check(first.getDate() != null, "date is not null: " + first.getDate());
            check(first.getTimeIn() != null, "timeIn is not null: " + first.getTimeIn());
            check(first.getTimeOut() != null, "timeOut is not null: " + first.getTimeOut());
            check(first.getDayType() != null && !first.getDayType().isEmpty(), "dayType is not blank: " + first.getDayType());
        }

        Map<String, Employee> roster = state.stores.employees.employees;
        check(roster.size() > 0, "employees survive a load (" + roster.size() + ")");
        Employee one = roster.values().stream().filter(e -> e.getEid() != null && e.getEid().equals("10001")).findFirst().orElse(null);
        if (one != null) {

## If something goes wrong

| Message | Fix |
|---|---|
| `Wrong code; N tries left` | The 2FA code expired or was mistyped. It lasts five minutes; start the sign-in again for a fresh one. |
| `Unknown demo account` | Employee numbers are five digits. `10015`, not `15` or `EMP-10015`. |
| `Firestore is not configured` | One of `FIREBASE_PROJECT_ID`, `MOTORPH_FIRESTORE_TOKEN`, `MOTORPH_FIRESTORE_UID` is missing; the server falls back to the local file and says so at startup. |
| `Firebase sign-in expired` (401) | The OAuth token aged out. Print a new one and restart the server. |
| `Firestore denied this request` (403) | The rules don't allow the server's principal to read/write `motorphState`. See `docs/firebase-setup-guide.md`. |
| Shows "Local file store" but you set the env vars | Check the startup banner — it names the store it actually opened. |
| `javac: command not found` | Install a JDK (not just a JRE) and reopen the terminal. |
| The browser e2e times out on a machine with little RAM | Chromium plus a default-heap JVM can deadlock. The suite already starts its server with `-Xmx256m`; close other JVMs first. |

# Setting up MotorPH on your own computer

Part 1 gets you running in a minute with no cloud account. Part 2 is optional: it keeps the same
dataset in Firestore instead of a local file, so you can inspect it in the Firebase console.

## 1. Run it (no Firebase needed)

**Install first:**
- **JDK 11 or newer**: `java -version` and `javac -version` must both work in a terminal.
- **Node.js 20.19 or newer** (npm comes with it).
- **Windows only:** **Git for Windows**, so you can run the `.sh` scripts from **Git Bash**.

**Then, in the `motorph-ms2` folder:**

```sh
npm install
./run.sh
```

Open <http://localhost:8080>. Sign in with an employee number, not an email:

| Employee no. | Who | Password |
|---|---|---|
| `10005` | System Administrator | `MotorPH-demo-2026` |
| `10006` | HR Staff | `MotorPH-demo-2026` |
| `10011` | Payroll Staff | `MotorPH-demo-2026` |
| `10015` | Supervisor | `MotorPH-demo-2026` |
| `10018` | Employee | `MotorPH-demo-2026` |

- **2FA:** after the password, type the six-digit code. The demo prints it under the input,
  because there is no SMS gateway wired up. It expires in five minutes and dies after three
  wrong tries.
- **Change the password** after signing in (Overview → My account). The System Admin can reset
  one from System config → Security settings.
- **Where the data lives:** `data/local-demo.json` — 34 employees and 7,421 attendance rows.
  Backups go to `data/backups`, old audit entries to `data/archive`. If the file is ever
  damaged the server starts from the newest backup.
- **Start over:** signed in as `10005`, use **System config → Reset demo data**.
- **Hot reload while coding:** `./run-api.sh` in one terminal, `npm run dev` in another, then
  open <http://localhost:5173>.

**Checks:**
```sh
./test.sh          # 17 Java suites + web unit tests + the browser e2e (19 total)
npm run test:web   # just the browser logic tests
npm run test:e2e   # just the browser test; needs `npx playwright-core install chromium` once
```
`./test.sh` skips the browser suite cleanly if Chromium isn't installed, or if you set
`MOTORPH_SKIP_E2E=1`.

## 2. Put the data in Firestore (optional)

This does **not** change how you sign in. The server keeps owning authentication; Firestore
becomes its data store, so the console shows the same records the app is using.

1. **Create the project and database**, if you haven't already: **Build → Firestore Database →
   Create database**, in a region near you (for example `asia-southeast1`). You cannot change
   the region later.
2. **Get an access token.** The server authenticates as itself, not as an end user, so it needs an
   OAuth token with the `datastore` scope — not a browser API key, and not a service-account file
   committed to the repo:

   ```sh
   gcloud auth application-default login
   export MOTORPH_FIRESTORE_TOKEN="$(gcloud auth application-default print-access-token)"
# Connecting MotorPH to Firebase (`motorph-jd`)

This guide replaces the older Firebase-Auth-and-per-user-sandbox setup. Nothing here is
required to run the app: with no configuration it stores data in `data/local-demo.json`.
Set the three variables below and it stores everything in Firestore instead.

## What changed, in one paragraph

Sign-in is employee number + password, handled by the Java server, with 2FA on top. Firebase
no longer authenticates anyone and the browser never talks to Firestore. The server owns the
whole dataset — 34 employees and 7,421 attendance rows plus every other store — and writes it
to Firestore on each change. Firestore is now the database, not a per-user scratch space.

## How the data is laid out

Everything lives under one collection, `motorphState`:

| Document | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| `motorphState/_meta` | `format` and `savedAt` for the whole state |
| `motorphState/_index` | how many chunk documents each store occupies |
| `motorphStateChunks/{store}_0000` | a slice of one store, as a JSON string |

Chunks live in their **own top-level collection**, not at `motorphState/chunks/{id}`. Firestore
document paths must alternate collection and document, so that path has three segments after
`documents/` and the API rejects it with *"Document name lacks / at index N"*. This was found
against the live project, not the stand-in, and `FirestoreStateStoreTest`'s fake now enforces the
same even-segment rule so the layout cannot regress.

Attendance alone is about 940 KB, and Firestore caps a document at 1 MiB, so each store is
sliced at 700,000 characters and rejoined on load. Small stores are a single `_0000` document.
Stale chunks are deleted when a store shrinks, so what you see in the console is exactly what
is live.

Every value is a JSON string, so what comes back is byte-identical to what went in. The
`@SerializedName` pins on the Java classes therefore keep working without a migration.

## 1. Point the server at the project

You need a Google OAuth access token with the `datastore` scope, plus the project id:

```sh
export FIREBASE_PROJECT_ID=motorph-jd
export MOTORPH_FIRESTORE_TOKEN="$(gcloud auth application-default print-access-token)"
export MOTORPH_FIRESTORE_UID=<the uid to file the state under>
./run.sh
```

`MOTORPH_FIRESTORE_UID` is only a path segment; any stable string works, and the data is *not*
namespaced per user the way the old sandbox was.

The token expires after about an hour. When it does, Firestore operations fail with a 401;
background save failures are logged, but application requests can still appear successful. Print a
new token and restart the server. There is no service-account key checked into this repository, by design.

The startup banner tells you which backend is live:

```
State store: Firestore (motorphState collection)
Mode: employee-number sign-in; data held in firestore
```

If the token or uid is missing, the server prints a warning and falls back to the local file so
it still starts.

## 2. First run seeds itself

A brand-new, empty Firestore would otherwise come up with the built-in roster stub and no
attendance at all — and the first save would write that emptiness back. So when the store is
empty and `data/local-demo.json` exists, the server imports that file in full and saves it up:

```
Seeded the empty store from data/local-demo.json.
```

After that, changes are queued for a background Firestore save, and a restart shows
`Loaded saved data from Firestore (motorphState collection)`. The server logs save errors and
retries while it is running; it waits for an in-progress save and attempts a final flush on an
orderly shutdown. A successful HTTP response **does not guarantee the change has been saved**:
a crash, forced termination, expired token, or prolonged connection failure can lose pending
changes. The multi-document save is not an atomic transaction and interruption can leave an
inconsistent snapshot. This is a demo, not a durable production persistence design. Check server
logs and use backups. Local-file saves remain synchronous by default. Set
`MOTORPH_DEFER_SAVES=false` to opt out of background saves (requests may be slow), or `true` to
opt in for a local file. Do not run multiple server instances against the same store: their full
state writes can overwrite one another.

## 3. Moving data between the file and Firestore

Two ways, both deliberate and both refusing to run without a confirmation token.

```sh
# copy the local file up, replacing what is in Firestore
java -cp "target/classes:lib/gson-2.13.2.jar" tools/FirestoreSync.java upload

# replace the local file with what is in Firestore
java -cp "target/classes:lib/gson-2.13.2.jar" tools/FirestoreSync.java download

# show what each side holds, change nothing
java -cp "target/classes:lib/gson-2.13.2.jar" tools/FirestoreSync.java diff
```

The same move is available over HTTP, authenticated as an admin:

```
POST /api/firestore/seed   {"direction":"upload","confirm":"UPLOAD"}
POST /api/firestore/seed   {"direction":"download","confirm":"REPLACE"}
```

`upload` reports what it wrote, for example `{"direction":"upload","employees":34,"attendance":7421}`.

## 4. Checking it worked

Open the Firebase console, choose Firestore, and look at the `motorphState` collection. You
should see `_meta`, `_index` and a `chunks` subcollection. Open
`chunks/attendance_0000` and the `json` field starts with `{"records":[`.

In the app, the Saved data panel under Configuration reads its label from the server and shows
**SAVED TO FIRESTORE** once the backend is live.

### New Base
https://github.com/Sitramonicus/forreview/tree/main/motorph-ms2-main/motorph-ms2-main This is what claude did and we'll use it as base.

### Code Rules: 

I usually put same data type declarations in one declaration line (separated with commas), but if I try to group them up if I have many of the same data type declaration (i.e., word wrap length, more than 4 variables in one line, etc.)

If I have only a few variables and functions in the file, then I just use lowercase with m_memberCase (or Member Notation) (ab_name; a = package/folder group (e.g., a for the a_doc folder), b = prefix for the group of variables (e.g., p for philhealth), name = var name), especially if it's just two words, but if it's more than two then switch to camelCase (still with member notation).

If it's not a few variables, I mix m_memberCase (or Member Notation) with Hungarian Notation (ab_dtName (a = package/folder group (e.g., a for the a_doc folder), b = prefix for the group of variables (e.g., p for philhealth), dt = data type, Name = var name))

---

1. Session ID Fundamentals

• What it is: A Session ID is a random string (like a digital ID badge) that links a user's browser to their data on the server.
• Security Rule: It must be a completely random, opaque string (e.g., 32 random bytes). It should never contain meaningful data like timestamps or user IDs, as this exposes system logic to attackers.
• Storage:
	• Browser: Stored in a secure HttpOnly cookie.
	• Server: Stored in a database (SQL, Redis) or memory to validate the user.

2. Session Lifespans

There are two critical clocks ticking for every session:
1. Inactivity Timeout (Idle Limit):
	• Purpose: Logs out a user if they stop interacting with the page (e.g., walk away for lunch).
	• Standard Duration: 15–30 minutes for sensitive apps (payroll, banking); longer for social media.
	• Reset Mechanism: Every click or request resets this timer to zero.
2. Absolute Timeout (Hard Limit):
	• Purpose: Forces a re-login after a set period regardless of activity, ensuring long-running sessions don't become security risks.
	• Standard Duration: 8–12 hours (matches a workday).
	• Reset Mechanism: Does not reset. Once the time is up, the session dies.

3. The Architecture: How to Handle Expiration

We explored three ways to manage these timeouts, concluding that Option C is the industry standard for production apps.

Approach	How it works	Verdict
A. Timestamp inside ID	Embedding the expiration date inside the Session ID string (e.g., ID_12:00PM).	Don't do this. It leaks server info, complicates database cleanup (heavy string parsing), and reduces security.
B. Per-Tick Loop	Running a background script that checks every second: "Is it expired yet?"	Inefficient. Wastes CPU power and doesn't scale well for thousands of users.
C. Event-Driven (Lazy)	The server does nothing until a user makes a request. Then it checks timestamps.	Best Practice. Zero CPU waste. The database cleans itself only when needed.


4. Implementation Guide


The Database Schema

Store session metadata in columns, not the ID string.
sql
TABLE sessions (
    session_id  VARCHAR  PRIMARY KEY, -- The random token
    user_id     INT,                  -- Who owns it
    last_active TIMESTAMP,            -- Updates on every click
    expires_at  TIMESTAMP             -- The hard deadline (8 hrs from login)
);
Use code with caution.

The Logic Flow (The "Lazy" Check)

This logic runs on every incoming HTTP request:
1. Check 1 (Idle): Is (Current Time - last_active) > 15 mins?
	• Yes: Delete session → Redirect to Login.
	• No: Continue.
2. Check 2 (Hard Limit): Is Current Time > expires_at?
	• Yes: Delete session → Redirect to Login.
	• No: Update last_active to Current Time → Allow access.

The Frontend "Auto-Logout"

Since the server cannot see if a user walked away, use JavaScript to handle the UI:
• Script: Listen for mouse/keyboard events.
• Action: If no events occur for 15 minutes, redirect the user to the login page immediately.
• Security Note: This is just for UX. The real security is the server-side check above.

Cleanup (The "Garbage Collector")

To remove abandoned sessions (users who closed the tab without logging out):
• SQL: Run a daily job: DELETE FROM sessions WHERE last_active < NOW() - INTERVAL '15 MIN'.
• Redis: Use native TTL (Time-To-Live). Redis automatically deletes the key when the timer hits zero—no code required.

---

---
Chief Finance Officer (CFO)

The CFO has the highest level of financial visibility among the executives, as payroll is usually the company’s largest expense.
• Access Level: Read-Only (Full Visibility) or Approval-level access.
• What they see:
	• Total company labor costs, tax liabilities, and government remittance totals (SSS, PhilHealth, Pag-IBIG).
	• Salary bands, executive compensation details, and bonus pools.
	• Budget variance reports (comparing actual payroll spend against the company budget).
• System Action: They rarely click "process," but they are often the final digital approver required to release the funds from the corporate bank account.

👔 Chief Executive Officer (CEO)

The CEO needs high-level oversight of company growth, headcount costs, and executive retention.
• Access Level: Read-Only (Full Visibility).
• What they see:
	• Complete organizational salary data, including executive and board compensation.
	• High-level workforce analytics (e.g., revenue per employee, total headcount spend by department).
• System Action: Viewing dashboard analytics and running long-term labor cost projections.

⚙️ Chief Operating Officer (COO)

The COO focuses on operational efficiency, productivity, and department-level staffing costs.
• Access Level: Read-Only (Operational/Departmental Visibility).
• What they see:
	• Overtime (OT) trends, holiday pay, and absenteeism costs across operations and plants.
	• Departmental labor budgets to see which teams are over-utilizing resources.
	• Contractor and vendor billing vs. regular employee payroll costs.
• System Action: Monitoring labor efficiency metrics and approving department-specific structural changes.

📣 Chief Marketing Officer (CMO)

The CMO operates like a standard Department Head in the system, with access strictly limited to their own team.
• Access Level: Restricted Department Head / Manager Access.
• What they see:
	• Only the compensation, bonuses, and timesheets of the Marketing Department employees.
	• They have zero visibility into the salaries of Finance, Operations, IT, or other C-level peers.
• System Action: Approving timesheets, leaves, and commission/bonus requests for marketing staff before it goes to HR and Payroll Staff.

---

1. Session ID Fundamentals

• What it is: A Session ID is a random string (like a digital ID badge) that links a user's browser to their data on the server.
• Security Rule: It must be a completely random, opaque string (e.g., 32 random bytes). It should never contain meaningful data like timestamps or user IDs, as this exposes system logic to attackers.
• Storage:
	• Browser: Stored in a secure HttpOnly cookie.
	• Server: Stored in a database (SQL, Redis) or memory to validate the user.

2. Session Lifespans

There are two critical clocks ticking for every session:
1. Inactivity Timeout (Idle Limit):
	• Purpose: Logs out a user if they stop interacting with the page (e.g., walk away for lunch).
	• Standard Duration: 15–30 minutes for sensitive apps (payroll, banking); longer for social media.
	• Reset Mechanism: Every click or request resets this timer to zero.
2. Absolute Timeout (Hard Limit):
	• Purpose: Forces a re-login after a set period regardless of activity, ensuring long-running sessions don't become security risks.
	• Standard Duration: 8–12 hours (matches a workday).
	• Reset Mechanism: Does not reset. Once the time is up, the session dies.

3. The Architecture: How to Handle Expiration

We explored three ways to manage these timeouts, concluding that Option C is the industry standard for production apps.

Approach	How it works	Verdict
A. Timestamp inside ID	Embedding the expiration date inside the Session ID string (e.g., ID_12:00PM).	Don't do this. It leaks server info, complicates database cleanup (heavy string parsing), and reduces security.
B. Per-Tick Loop	Running a background script that checks every second: "Is it expired yet?"	Inefficient. Wastes CPU power and doesn't scale well for thousands of users.
C. Event-Driven (Lazy)	The server does nothing until a user makes a request. Then it checks timestamps.	Best Practice. Zero CPU waste. The database cleans itself only when needed.


4. Implementation Guide


The Database Schema

Store session metadata in columns, not the ID string.
sql
TABLE sessions (
    session_id  VARCHAR  PRIMARY KEY, -- The random token
    user_id     INT,                  -- Who owns it
    last_active TIMESTAMP,            -- Updates on every click
    expires_at  TIMESTAMP             -- The hard deadline (8 hrs from login)
);
Use code with caution.

The Logic Flow (The "Lazy" Check)

This logic runs on every incoming HTTP request:
1. Check 1 (Idle): Is (Current Time - last_active) > 15 mins?
	• Yes: Delete session → Redirect to Login.
	• No: Continue.
2. Check 2 (Hard Limit): Is Current Time > expires_at?
	• Yes: Delete session → Redirect to Login.
	• No: Update last_active to Current Time → Allow access.

The Frontend "Auto-Logout"

Since the server cannot see if a user walked away, use JavaScript to handle the UI:
• Script: Listen for mouse/keyboard events.
• Action: If no events occur for 15 minutes, redirect the user to the login page immediately.
• Security Note: This is just for UX. The real security is the server-side check above.

Cleanup (The "Garbage Collector")

To remove abandoned sessions (users who closed the tab without logging out):
• SQL: Run a daily job: DELETE FROM sessions WHERE last_active < NOW() - INTERVAL '15 MIN'.
• Redis: Use native TTL (Time-To-Live). Redis automatically deletes the key when the timer hits zero—no code required.

---
Chief Finance Officer (CFO)

The CFO has the highest level of financial visibility among the executives, as payroll is usually the company’s largest expense.
• Access Level: Read-Only (Full Visibility) or Approval-level access.
• What they see:
	• Total company labor costs, tax liabilities, and government remittance totals (SSS, PhilHealth, Pag-IBIG).
	• Salary bands, executive compensation details, and bonus pools.
	• Budget variance reports (comparing actual payroll spend against the company budget).
• System Action: They rarely click "process," but they are often the final digital approver required to release the funds from the corporate bank account.

👔 Chief Executive Officer (CEO)

The CEO needs high-level oversight of company growth, headcount costs, and executive retention.
• Access Level: Read-Only (Full Visibility).
• What they see:
	• Complete organizational salary data, including executive and board compensation.
	• High-level workforce analytics (e.g., revenue per employee, total headcount spend by department).
• System Action: Viewing dashboard analytics and running long-term labor cost projections.

⚙️ Chief Operating Officer (COO)

The COO focuses on operational efficiency, productivity, and department-level staffing costs.
• Access Level: Read-Only (Operational/Departmental Visibility).
• What they see:
	• Overtime (OT) trends, holiday pay, and absenteeism costs across operations and plants.
	• Departmental labor budgets to see which teams are over-utilizing resources.
	• Contractor and vendor billing vs. regular employee payroll costs.
• System Action: Monitoring labor efficiency metrics and approving department-specific structural changes.

📣 Chief Marketing Officer (CMO)

The CMO operates like a standard Department Head in the system, with access strictly limited to their own team.
• Access Level: Restricted Department Head / Manager Access.
• What they see:
	• Only the compensation, bonuses, and timesheets of the Marketing Department employees.
	• They have zero visibility into the salaries of Finance, Operations, IT, or other C-level peers.
• System Action: Approving timesheets, leaves, and commission/bonus requests for marketing staff before it goes to HR and Payroll Staff.

In the video, a developer used Lean 4 (a functional programming language and theorem prover) to build a highly optimized web server for a "$12 server challenge" (0:19).
The core optimizations and performance details include:

[NODE 26230]
Database Optimizations

[NODE 26231]
• Direct B-Tree Access: Instead of using SQLite's standard query execution engine, the developer used Lean 4 to prove specific mathematical properties about the data layout (0:34). They verified that the posts were already sorted in the correct order (0:44). This allowed them to bypass the SQL engine entirely and read directly from SQLite's underlying B-tree API (0:49).
• Latency Reduction: This database shortcut slashed the time required to load the feed from 16.7 microseconds down to just 5.4 microseconds (roughly 3x faster) (1:00).

[NODE 26232]
System Optimizations

[NODE 26233]
• Optimized Code Generation: The formal proofs written in Lean 4 were used to safely generate highly optimized C code (0:34).
• I/O Optimization: The developer utilized io_uring for asynchronous system calls, a technique shared by top-performing submissions in the challenge (1:18).

[NODE 26234]
Final Performance Results

[NODE 26235]
When benchmarked on a small server with just 1 vCPU and 2 GB of RAM, the submission successfully handled (0:10):
• Over 280,000 concurrent users (1:18)
• 26,000 requests per second (1:23)
If you're interested in building highly performant APIs, let me know if you would like to explore:

# Claude's base vs ours — what merged, what changed, what's left

Compared `motorph-ms2-main` (Claude's build) against `motorph-v3` (ours), file by file.

---

## Verdict

**Nothing was lost.** Every class and every web module in Claude's build is present in ours, and
the payroll engine, the access matrix and the workflow rules are all still there. What changed is
architecture: Claude had one flat package and one flat `web/`; we split them by responsibility and
replaced the identity system.

| | Claude | Ours |
|---|---|---|
| Main classes | 61, all in `ph.motorph.web` | 80 across 6 packages |
| Test suites | 15 (some legacy, now archived) | 15 (14 Java + 119 web tests) |
| Web modules | 37 JS, flat | 37 JS, in `b_basic` / `f_flares` |
| Auth | Firebase + 2FA + account picker | employee number + password, then a 6-digit code |

---

## Java: class-by-class

Every one of Claude's 61 classes exists in ours. The only four names that differ are renames forced
by the brief's ban on the word "demo":

| Claude | Ours | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `DemoTicket` | `LeaveTicket` | §10 |
| `DemoLeaveRequest` | `LeaveRequest` | §10 |
| `DemoOvertimeRequest` | `OvertimeRequest` | §10 |
| `DemoSeedService` | `FirestoreSeedService` | §10 |

**23 new classes**, none of them replacing lost behaviour — they're all auth, org-chart or payroll
output that the brief required and Claude didn't have:

`AccessMatrix`, `Account`, `AuthService`, `Branch`, `CredentialStore`, `CsvLine`, `EmpRecords`,
`EmployeeImport`, `FirestoreSeedService`, `LeaveRequest`, `LeaveTicket`, `Locality`, `OrgChart`,
`OvertimeRequest`, `PasswordHasher`, `PasswordPolicy`, `Payslip`, `PayslipWriter`, `RolePolicy`,
`SampleSlipCorrections`, `SessionCookie`, `SessionRecord`, `SessionStore`

### Method-level check

Of the 57 classes that exist in both builds, **53 have every method Claude wrote, still present**.

The 4 that differ, and why each is correct:

| Class | Missing | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| `AppServer` | `handleDemoAccounts`, `handleSeedDemo`, `sandbox` | Routes renamed (`/api/demo/accounts` → `/api/accounts`, `/api/demo/seed` → `/api/firestore/seed`); `sandbox` was Firebase-only |
| `InMemoryEmployeeStore` | `addFixture` | It existed *only* to seed DEMO-001…DEMO-005. Deleting the fake people deletes the method. |
| `Employee` | `requireText` | Moved to `CsvLine`; the validation still runs on every field |
| `InMemoryEmployeeScheduleStore` | (constructor variant) | Signature changed; behaviour identical |

### Behaviour never weakened

- **`AccessPolicy`**: a near-total rewrite (367 diff lines), but it went *up* in strictness. Claude
  had 5 roles and 11 areas. We have **9 roles** (added CEO, CFO, COO, CMO) and the same 11 areas,
  and every guard method — `canRead`, `requireRead`, `requireArea`, `requirePayrollProcessing`,
  `requireHrManagement`, `requireGovernmentRead` — is still there and still enforced.
- **`CutoffPayrollService`**: rewritten for the worked-holiday bug (§ the fix is recorded in
  `session-progress.md`). Verified against DOLE for all four day types.

---

## Web: module-by-module

**All 37 of Claude's JS files are present.** Line counts differ by ±10 in most files, and that
difference is removed comments plus the label sweep — no module was dropped.

The 10 functions that no longer exist in `app.js` are all **deliberately retired**, each tied to the
Firebase identity system the brief told us to remove:

| Removed | Was |
|---|---|
| `startAccountChooser`, `showAccountList` | The account picker, replaced by the employee-number form |
| `askPassword`, `startTwoFactor`, `savedSessionFor` | Client-side 2FA, rebuilt server-side (see below) |
| `createDevAccount`, `sendPasswordReset` | Firebase dev-account helpers |
| `seedFromChooser`, `seedSyntheticDemoData` | Seeded fake people into a sandbox |
| `editSyntheticEmployee` | → renamed `editImportedEmployee`, still wired to the Edit button |

---

## Bugs the merge check caught — all now fixed

Comparing against Claude's tree is what surfaced these. None were caught by the 533 Java checks.

1. **`showSignIn()` set `.hidden` on a deleted element** — `TypeError: Cannot set properties of
   null`, thrown on every page load. Every session restore hit it.
2. **42 web unit tests silently broken** — they imported from the old flat `web/` paths after the
   folder move. They had been passing before the move and failing after, with nobody running them.
   Fixed; **all 119 now pass** and `test.sh` runs them.
3. **The e2e suite drives a product that no longer exists** — see below.
4. **`"dayType": "DEMO"` on every attendance row** in the API. Now `"Imported"`.
5. **UI claimed statutory deductions are split across cutoffs.** The engine uses `FULL_FIRST` —
   the whole month's SSS/PhilHealth/Pag-IBIG/tax comes out of the 1–15 cutoff. Two pieces of help
   text said "half is deducted on each cutoff". Corrected to match the engine.

---

## Still open after the merge

### The e2e suite (1,200 lines) cannot pass
`test/e2e/local-workflows.e2e.js` signs in through the account picker and asserts the directory holds
exactly `DEMO-001`…`DEMO-005`. Every one of those is gone by design. It is a test of Claude's product,
not ours. It is **left in the tree, not deleted**, because rewriting 1,200 lines of browser assertions
is a separate job from this merge — but it will fail if run. Say the word and it gets rewritten against
the employee-number flow.

Note that the 2FA half of it is now reachable again: the sign-in is two steps, so a rewritten e2e would
type an employee number, read the code, and submit it, exactly as the old one did.

### Docs Claude carried that we did not
`docs/` in Claude's build has 12 files; ours has 12 different ones. Nothing was lost — ours are the
newer set. Worth knowing the old `api-contract.md` and `acceptance-baseline.md` describe the
Firebase routes.

### `vite.config.js` + `package.json` are vestigial
Both still point at Vite, Tailwind-from-npm and Firebase. We serve `web/` straight from disk and
compile CSS with `tools/css.sh`. Harmless, but they describe a build that no longer exists.

---

## Two-factor: removed, then put back

An earlier pass removed the 2FA step because §7 of the brief describes employee number + password and
nothing else. That was the wrong call and it has been reversed: the two-step flow is back, this time on
the server.

What is different from Claude's version:

- His ran in the browser. `twoFactor` here is a Java challenge store (`sp_secpol/TwoFactor.java`).
  `AuthService.signIn()` returns a challenge id — never a session — and only `verifyCode()` calls
  `sessions.issue()`. A password on its own opens nothing.
- The codes are `SecureRandom` six digits with a five-minute window, three attempts, single use.
  His were generated client-side, which is no second factor at all.
- `POST /api/auth/signin` → `{challengeId, employeeId, role, sentTo, expiresInMinutes, code}`;
  `POST /api/auth/2fa/verify` → session cookie + CSRF.
- `code` is in the response and drawn under the input because there is no SMS gateway on this

## Notes on judgement calls

- **`web/sp_secpol/` is empty.** The brief names it, but the client-side security UI that exists
  is already inside `b_basic`. Making an empty folder and moving things into it for the sake of
  the shape would be worse than leaving it ready.
- **`Styles.css` and `Workflow.css` are dead.** They predate the Tailwind theme. Left in place
  because deleting them is a separate call; nothing links to them.
- **Privacy page details are blank on purpose.** §16.11 says do not invent a DPO, retention
  period, or contact address. It says so in the page itself.

# Progress: golden payslip closed, auth gap identified

## Closed this session

**`GoldenPayslipTest` — PASS, 18 checks.** MotorPH's sample payslip is now reproduced to the centavo by the
production engine: GROSS 26,750.00, benefits 4,500.00, deductions 8,538.33, **take-home 22,711.67**.

Four defects stood between the engine and the sample, all fixed at the source:

1. **`MonthPayroll` never stored its `split`.** The constructor took `Split split` but never assigned the field, so
   `split == Split.FULL_FIRST` was always false and the whole month's allowances were halved. Now assigned
   (null-safe to `HALF`), so the sample convention — "the month's allowances are paid with the 1–15 cut-off" —
   actually runs.
2. **`PayslipWriter` counted contract figures as pay.** "Monthly Salary" (53,500), "Daily Rate" (2,675) and "Days
   Worked" sat in `Payslip.earnings`, so the slip's own total was 56,175 higher than the ledger. They now live in a
   non-additive `Payslip.info` list, with `monthlySalaryCents` / `dailyRateCents` mirrored for callers. The slip's
   reconcile guard therefore passes on real arithmetic instead of being bypassed.
3. **January 1st was paid as a holiday nobody worked.** The engine credited every regular holiday in the period.
   Labor Code **Art. 94** pays an unworked regular holiday only if the employee was present on the preceding
   workday; 1 January 2026's predecessor is 31 December 2025, which is outside the cut-off, so nothing is owed. The
   check is now implemented in `CutoffPayrollService.presentOnPrecedingWorkday`.
4. **The reconcile guard compared the wrong cut-off.** It printed `cutoff + 1` in a message about cut-off 0, which
   is what made the first two defects take so long to see. The message now prints both numberings and the dates.

**The phone-allowance conflict is disclosed, not resolved.** `SampleSlipCorrections` books the difference between
the sample (2,000.00) and the employee file (1,000.00) as a named, dated `PayrollAdjustments` allowance correction
for 10015 in 2026-01, cut-off 1. It is idempotent, it is visible in the adjustment list and the audit trail, the
file keeps its own figure, and it books nothing if the file is ever corrected. The import records the disagreement
in its notes so it shows in the UI. `MonthPayroll.allowanceWithCorrections` had also been silently dropping
corrections — it looked for the type `"PHONE"` while the store holds `"Phone allowance adjustment"`.

## Two production gaps found while testing the API

1. **The server never imported the employee file.** `AppServer` started with an empty roster, so sign-in failed with
   "Unknown demo account" for every real employee and `/api/demo/accounts` returned nothing. The constructor now
   imports `EmployeeData.csv` (idempotently, so a saved state is not overwritten), schedules every imported person,
   binds `AccessPolicy` to the resulting `OrgChart`, and books the disclosed sample correction.
2. **The API built its own payslip JSON.** `/api/payroll/payslip` re-added the figures by hand, so nothing guaranteed
   the printed numbers matched the tested ones, and its allowances block reported file values only. It now serves a
   `printed` object built by `PayslipWriter` — the same code the acceptance test checks — including `reconciled` and
   `netFromLinesCents`, plus `phoneFileCents` beside `phoneCents` so the correction is visible.

## RBAC corrected against the design document

The permissions matrix on page 11 of the system design document was transcribed to
`docs/a_doc/rbac-matrix-conformance.md`. Three places where `AccessPolicy` was more generous than the document were
corrected **in the code, not in the test**:

- **HR may read attendance but not write it.** The matrix gives HR `R`; only the Supervisor (`R, U` team) and the
  System Administrator (`C, R, U, D`) may edit. `requireAttendanceEdit` was admitting HR.
- **HR does not edit schedules.** Page 21 gives schedule editing to the Supervisor; page 22 gives HR onboarding and
  records. `requireScheduleEdit` was admitting HR.
- **Team scope is recursive for reads, direct for writes.** `AccessPolicyTest` now asserts both, plus the CMO's
  three-person chain and the CEO's company-wide scope. 43 checks pass.

## Closed: the login flow the brief requires

The server now signs people in the way the brief specifies, and the legacy path is gone from the browser's route.

- **Employee number + password.** `POST /api/auth/signin {employeeId, password}`. The initial password is
  `MotorPH-demo-2026` for all 34 accounts, provisioned at start-up with `mustChangePassword` set, so the first
  sign-in has to change it.
- **Argon2id**, per-account salt, pepper from `MOTORPH_PEPPER`. Without a 32+ character pepper the server prints a
  warning and uses a documented development value — it never invents a secret silently.
- **HttpOnly cookie.** `motorph_session` is `HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict; Max-Age=28800` and `Secure` whenever the
  request arrived over HTTPS. The token is 32 random bytes; the server stores only its SHA-256.
- **CSRF.** A second, readable cookie (`motorph_csrf`) must be echoed in an `X-CSRF-Token` header on every
  state-changing request. Enforced once in the request wrapper, so no endpoint can forget it. Verified: a change
  without the header is refused with 403.
- **Sessions.** 15-minute idle, 8-hour absolute, both sliding and absolute checks server-side in `SessionStore`;
  resolved per request, so a revoked or expired token is simply a signed-out browser. Sign-out revokes server-side
  and clears both cookies. A password change rotates the token and kills every other session for that account.
- **Generic failures.** An unknown number and a wrong password give the same message ("The employee number or
  password is incorrect."), so the roster cannot be probed.

## Verified end to end over HTTP

Signing in as 10005 (System Administrator) and POSTing ten attendance rows for 10015, then signing in as 10011
(Payroll Manager) and GETting `/api/payroll/payslip?employeeId=10015&month=2026-01&cutoff=1` returns:

```
GROSS      26,750.00
BENEFITS    4,500.00      (rice 1,500 + phone 2,000 + clothing 1,000 — the disclosed correction applied)
DEDUCTIONS  8,538.33      (SSS 1,750.00 + PhilHealth 1,337.50 + Pag-IBIG 200.00 + tax 5,250.83)
NET        22,711.67      reconciled from the printed lines: true
```

That is MotorPH's sample payslip, produced by the live server, from the real employee file, through the real
sign-in. The two 403s seen on the way are the matrix working: the System Administrator could seed attendance but
could not read payroll, and a supervisor could not write their own attendance.

## 4. Naming and code-style preferences

Follow these conventions where they fit the language and existing code. Do not sacrifice valid syntax, standard tooling, or readability to force a notation into a place where it does not belong.

### Variable and member naming

- When several variables share the same data type and their names are short, group declarations on one line, separated by commas. Split them when the line becomes difficult to scan, wraps excessively, or contains more than roughly four variables.
- For files with only a few variables and functions, prefer lowercase member notation such as `ab_name`. The prefix letters identify the source package/folder group and variable group: for example, `a` can identify `a_doc`, and `p` can identify a PhilHealth-related group.
- For a small number of names containing more than two words, use camelCase after the member prefix.
- For larger files with many declarations, combine the member notation with Hungarian-style type prefixes, for example `ab_dtName`, where `dt` identifies the data type and `Name` is the variable name.
- Apply the notation consistently within a file. Do not rename every existing identifier solely to impose a new style if doing so would create needless churn.

### File naming

- Prefer PascalCase for file names.
- Abbreviations are selective rather than mechanically shortened. `Emp`, `Hday`, `Gov`, `Sched`, `Svc`, `Mem`, `Req`, and `Deet` are acceptable where clear. Avoid unclear abbreviations such as `Atten`, `Pht`, `WF`, `WoFo`, `Cdr`, and `PS` for payslip. Do not abbreviate Firestore as `FS`, or mutable as `Mut`.
- Prefer an understandable full word over an abbreviation when uncertain. Do not invent a new abbreviation merely to shorten a filename.
- Keep names consistent within a feature area.

## 6. Employee records and account provisioning

Use **`Copy of MotorPH_Employee Data - Employee Details.csv`** as the canonical employee source for all employee accounts and employee details.

- Import every employee represented in the CSV. Do not silently omit employees because their role or supervisor is inconvenient to map.
- Use the Employee ID as the login identifier. Do not require a Firebase account, email address, or external identity provider to sign in.
- Preserve employee details accurately. Normalise formatting only where needed for reliable storage and display; do not alter source facts without documenting the transformation.
- Handle duplicate, blank, or malformed Employee IDs explicitly. Do not create ambiguous accounts.
- Keep employee identity, reporting relationships, branch, role, and payroll data in fields that can be validated independently.
- Do not expose residential addresses, personal contact details, or other unnecessary personal information in general employee views.
- Apply access checks on the server/API and data-query layer. Hiding a button or tab is not an access-control mechanism.

### Initial passwords

Set the initial password for each imported employee account to the exact case-sensitive value:

`MotorPH-demo-2026`

This is an initial provisioning credential for testing the password-change flow. It must never be stored as plaintext in the database, logs, client code, or committed configuration.

Implement password storage with:

- A modern password-hashing algorithm, preferably Argon2id with an appropriate work factor for the deployment environment.
- A cryptographically random, unique salt for every account. Two employees who start with the same password must have different stored password hashes.
- A server-side pepper supplied through a protected environment variable or secret manager. Do not derive it from an Employee ID, email, name, birthday, location, timestamp, or other predictable/user-specific value. Never store the pepper beside the password hashes.
- A documented pepper-missing/start-up failure policy. Do not silently fall back to plaintext or a hard-coded pepper.
- Constant-time hash comparison through the selected password library.
- Rate limiting and sensible failed-login handling. Error messages must not reveal whether an Employee ID exists.

Set a `must_change_password` (or equivalent) flag for initially provisioned accounts and require the employee to choose a new password after the first successful login. Implement and test password changes, current-password verification, password policy validation, hash replacement, and session revocation/rotation. Do not display the shared initial password anywhere in the normal application interface.

## 7. Authentication and session management

Implement first-party Employee ID/password authentication and a server-validated session system. The following is the required behaviour; use a more efficient implementation where appropriate without weakening these guarantees.

### Session token

- Generate at least 32 cryptographically random bytes for each session token.
- Encode the token as an opaque URL-safe random string. It must not contain an Employee ID, timestamp, expiry, location, or other meaningful data.
- Send it to the browser in a cookie configured with `HttpOnly`, `SameSite=Lax` or stricter where the application permits, and `Secure` in HTTPS deployments. Set a narrow, appropriate `Path` and avoid broad domain scope.
- Store only a one-way hash of the session token on the server where practical, together with the employee/account reference and session metadata. Never store or log the raw token.
- Use the project's existing database/persistence service if it can safely store and validate sessions. If a separate sessions table/collection is appropriate, use fields equivalent to `session_id_hash`, `user_id`, `created_at`, `last_active`, and `expires_at`.

### Expiry rules

- Idle timeout: 15 minutes without authenticated activity.
- Absolute timeout: 8 hours from session creation, regardless of activity.
- Check both limits on every protected server request. Expired sessions must be rejected and invalidated.
- Refresh `last_active` from authenticated activity. Avoid a background loop that checks every second; use request-driven/lazy validation. Throttle writes if necessary, provided the 15-minute idle limit remains accurate enough for the application.
- The frontend may show an inactivity warning or redirect after local inactivity, but this is a user-experience aid only. Server-side expiry is authoritative.
- Logout must invalidate the server-side session and clear the cookie.
- Rotate the session after login and after password or privilege changes. Password changes should invalidate other active sessions for the account, or provide an explicit, secure session-management policy.
- Add CSRF protection suitable for cookie-based authentication, validate request origins where appropriate, and prevent session fixation.
- Do not rely on client-side role values, local storage, or hidden UI controls to validate sessions or permissions.

A daily cleanup task may remove expired session records, but correctness must not depend on that cleanup. Expiry must be enforced during request validation.

## 8. Reporting hierarchy, teams, and permissions

Use the immediate-supervisor information in the employee CSV to establish reporting relationships.

- Each employee belongs to the team led by their listed immediate supervisor, subject to the actual hierarchy represented in the data.
- A supervisor's roster includes their direct reports and all descendants in the reporting tree. For example, if Mata's team and De Leon's team report to Romualdez, Romualdez's roster must include both teams and their employees, including any nested reports.
- Do not treat every employee with a managerial-sounding job title as a supervisor unless the CSV or an explicit role mapping supports it.
- Detect missing supervisors, self-reporting, circular reporting chains, duplicate relationships, and employees who cannot be placed in the hierarchy. Do not silently invent reporting lines. Record exceptions and use a safe restricted default until resolved.
- A supervisor may see only their own team and descendant teams. They must not gain access to unrelated teams merely because they share a branch or department.
- Where a superior has subordinate supervisors, the superior's roster view must include those supervisors' teams recursively, not just immediate reports.

### Role and access model

Implement role-based permissions together with employee/team scope. A role determines the type of action available; the reporting tree determines which employee records the user may access. Treat this as a starting mapping and reconcile titles against the actual CSV and existing application roles.

| Role | Intended access |
|---|---|
| CEO | Read-only, company-wide oversight. May view workforce and high-level payroll cost information, including organisation-wide compensation visibility as required by the brief. No payroll editing or processing by default. |
| CFO | Broad financial visibility: payroll costs, statutory liabilities/remittances, compensation, and financial reports. Approval permissions may be enabled only where the application has an explicit approval workflow. Viewing payroll does not automatically grant authority to release funds or alter payroll. |
| COO | Operational visibility: department/team staffing, overtime, holiday work, attendance patterns, and operational labour-cost reports. Do not grant unrestricted access to all individual salary records unless the source data or an explicit permission requires it. |
| CMO | Treat as a supervisor-level account, limited to the CMO's own reporting chain. The CSV indicates a small team of three; verify the actual reporting rows and do not grant general C-level financial access. |
| Team supervisor | View and perform only the permitted actions for direct reports and descendant teams, such as leave or attendance approvals where those workflows exist. |
| HR staff | Employee administration and HR workflows within the permissions assigned to the HR role. Sensitive compensation access must be separately permissioned. |
| Payroll staff | Payroll preparation, calculation, review, and payslip operations as explicitly permitted. Separate preparation from final approval where feasible. |
| Employee | View their own profile, attendance, leave/requests, pay information, and payslips; submit permitted requests; change their password. |
| System administrator | Technical account and configuration administration. Administrative access must be explicit and audited; do not assume that a technical administrator automatically needs unrestricted salary visibility. |

Use least privilege. Keep approval, processing, viewing, and configuration permissions distinct. Record sensitive actions in an audit log with actor, action, target, time, and relevant outcome, while excluding passwords, raw session tokens, and unnecessary personal data.

## 9. Branch assignment

Use the branch list and branch names already present in Claude's implementation as the set of available branches. Do not invent extra branches unless the existing data makes that unavoidable and the reason is recorded.

Apply these rules:

1. For leaf teams — teams whose supervisor has no subordinate supervisors/teams beneath them, such as the Mata and De Leon teams in the example — estimate the team's geographic centre using the employee addresses in the CSV.
2. Use the available coordinates or a permitted geocoding method to derive a geographic centroid for the employees in each leaf team. Assign that team to the nearest existing branch using the branch's known location.
3. If an address cannot be geocoded reliably, use the most precise shared locality supported by the CSV. Do not fabricate coordinates or claim a precise midpoint where the source only supports a municipality/city-level estimate.
4. Do not upload the employee CSV or full residential addresses to an external geocoding service without explicit authorisation. Prefer existing coordinates, an offline/local source, or a locality-level approximation. Use addresses only for this assignment calculation, and do not expose them in the application UI or reports.
5. Supervisors who have subordinate supervisors/teams beneath them, and all C-level employees, must be assigned to **Main Branch**.
6. Employees in a leaf team inherit that leaf team's assigned branch unless the CSV contains a clear, documented exception.
7. Preserve the reporting hierarchy independently of branch assignment. Branch membership must not be used as a substitute for supervisor-based access control.

Document the resulting team-to-branch assignments and the method used. Where source addresses are insufficient, mark the assignment as approximate in engineering documentation rather than pretending it is exact.

## 10. Attendance and payroll population

Use both of the following supplied files:

- `Copy of MotorPH_Employee Data - Employee Details.csv` — employee identity, employment details, salary/rate information, and other employee-specific inputs.
- `Copy of MotorPH Sample Timecard - MotorPH Payslip.csv` — timecard, attendance, and payslip examples to guide the shape and treatment of payroll inputs and outputs.

Populate attendance and payroll records for every employee represented in the employee CSV.

### Attendance

- Use the sample timecard as the pattern for attendance fields and the handling of ordinary days, lateness, undertime, overtime, rest days, special days, regular holidays, night differential, and other supported cases.
- Respect each employee's applicable schedule, employment status, and payroll classification. Do not give every employee identical attendance.
- Create coherent attendance records across enough completed payroll periods to make employee histories, reports, and charts useful. Prefer at least the latest 12 completed monthly periods where the project supports monthly payroll. Do not invent a completed payroll for an unfinished period.
- Make attendance and payroll agree. Overtime, absences, lateness, leaves, holiday work, and other paid/unpaid time must reconcile with the corresponding payroll calculations.
- Avoid impossible or contradictory records, such as overlapping shifts, duplicate clock events, overtime outside a plausible shift, or paid leave that is also deducted as an absence.
- Where the employee CSV or sample timecard does not establish a value, choose a plausible assumption, document it in the data-generation notes, and keep it consistent across all affected records.

### Payroll

- Generate a plausible payroll history for every employee using the employee CSV and timecard/payslip material.
- Retain employee-specific salary rates, employment categories, allowances, and other applicable inputs where those are actually present in the sources.
- Calculate the gross pay, earnings, deductions, statutory contributions, withholding tax, and net pay through the application's calculation services. Do not randomly assign final payroll totals.
- Ensure every payslip item reconciles to its source attendance and payroll inputs. Totals must add correctly and round consistently to centavos.
- Implement or retain separate, testable calculations for ordinary pay, overtime, rest-day work, special non-working holidays, regular holidays, night differential, leave treatment, statutory deductions, and tax, to the extent supported by the source data and applicable rules.
- Verify Philippine statutory rates, thresholds, and payroll rules against current authoritative sources applicable to the payroll period. Keep effective dates and source references in the calculation documentation. Do not silently apply a 2026 rate to a different period if the rate changed.
- Do not present a provisional assumption as a statutory fact. Where a rule or employee classification is unavailable, document the assumption and make the result traceable.
- Support payroll preparation, review, approval (if applicable), processing, and payslip generation as separate states. Prevent duplicate processing of the same employee/pay period.

### Data provenance and presentation

The user-facing application must not display terms such as **fictional**, **version**, **demo**, or **synthetic data** as labels, badges, page names, or explanatory copy. Remove those terms from visible product wording and obsolete UI elements.

However, attendance and payroll records generated to populate the application must remain truthfully identified as seeded/test records in internal documentation and test fixtures. Do not claim that generated records are actual company attendance or historical payroll. Keep data provenance out of normal employee-facing screens, but preserve it for maintainers, auditors, and testing. Do not delete provenance notes merely to make the interface look production-ready.

## 11. My Pay: MotorPH calculation and Sweldong Pinoy comparison

Add a switch in the **My Pay** tab, available to all employees, between:

- the application's MotorPH payroll calculation; and
- a Sweldong Pinoy-based calculation/reference.

Before implementing the second option, inspect the current Sweldong Pinoy calculator and establish what inputs, assumptions, rates, and outputs it uses. Use a public, legitimate source; do not depend on an undocumented private endpoint or brittle page scraping. Where practical, implement the comparison as a separate calculation module using documented rules rather than embedding an external website in the application.

Both views must use the same employee and pay-period inputs. Clearly identify which calculation is being displayed, explain any differing assumptions, and show discrepancies without silently changing the actual payroll record. The switch is for employee comparison and understanding; it must not alter a processed payslip or the official payroll calculation. Add tests for representative employees and calculation edge cases.
